title: Wawancara dengan Aktivis Muda Food Not Bombs di Rusia
content:
Oleh: 

Citizen Ilya

. Teks aslinya berjudul “

An Interview with Young Russian Activists from Food Not Bombs

”. Diterj

emahkan ke dalam Bahasa Indonesia oleh Ameyuri Ringo.




Support Ameyuri Ringo by considering becoming his 

Patron

.




Food Not Bombs adalah gerakan internasional independen yang melakukan aksi langsung dengan membagikan makanan vegan kepada siapa saja yang membutuhkan. Para aktivisnya percaya bahwa kegiatan ini merupakan bagian dari perjuangan melawan kemiskinan, militerisme, dan kekerasan. Seluruh kelompok Food Not Bombs yang ada di Rusia beroperasi secara terdesentralisasi, tetapi tetap berpegang pada gagasan yang sama. Di tengah situasi ketika pemerintah Rusia menghabiskan miliaran rubel untuk anggaran militer, setidaknya 20 juta orang masih hidup di bawah garis kemiskinan. Kehadiran para aktivis antifasis muda ini telah membawa perubahan bagi banyak orang. Kami menghubungi beberapa aktivis Food Not Bombs di Samara untuk berbincang mengenai gerakan mereka.




1. Bisa ceritakan bagaimana gerakan ini muncul di Samara dan nilai-nilai apa yang kalian perjuangkan?




Andrew: 

Gerakan ini mulai muncul di Samara pada tahun 2000-an. Saat itu para aktivis harus menghadapi serangan kelompok neo-Nazi. Mereka turun ke jalan dengan tutup panci di satu tangan dan pisau di tangan lainnya, mempertahankan diri dari serangan para neo-Nazi.




Kini situasinya sudah berubah. Jalanan jauh lebih aman, berkat mereka yang dahulu berani melawan para pelaku kekerasan tersebut. Generasi antifasis pun telah berganti.




Kami mulai mengorganisir kegiatan ini untuk menunjukkan bahwa orang-orang bisa melakukan kebaikan tanpa bergantung pada negara. Banyak dari kami merupakan pendukung komunisme libertarian, sementara banyak yang lain sekadar karena tidak bisa tinggal diam melihat penderitaan sesama.




Sekitar awal 2016 kami mulai aktif sebagai relawan, terutama dengan membantu tempat penampungan hewan. Pada Agustus 2018 kami mulai mempelajari pengalaman aktivis di Moskow dan St. Petersburg yang membagikan makanan kepada mereka yang membutuhkan. Pada akhir Oktober kami mengadakan aksi pertama. Sejak saat itu kami terus berjalan dengan mengandalkan sumber daya dan kemampuan kami sendiri, sambil perlahan membangun kekuatan bersama.




Oleg: 

Gerakan ini sebenarnya berawal pada dekade 1980-an dan sejak itu menyebar ke berbagai belahan dunia, termasuk Rusia. Samara bukan pengecualian. Sepuluh hingga lima belas tahun lalu, aksi serupa juga pernah diadakan di kota ini. Kami hanya berusaha menghidupkannya kembali.




Tujuan utama gerakan ini adalah menarik perhatian publik terhadap kebijakan destruktif banyak pemerintah di dunia, yang menghabiskan dana besar untuk militer sementara jumlah orang miskin dan tunawisma terus bertambah akibat perang yang dimulai atau didukung oleh para penguasa.




Pada suatu titik, banyak dari kami merasa perlu melakukan sesuatu yang nyata daripada sekadar mengeluh tentang buruknya keadaan. Karena kami semua pernah mendengar tentang Food Not Bombs, kami memutuskan untuk menjalankan kegiatan semacam ini. Kami yakin kami mampu melakukannya, dan ternyata benar.




Masalahnya, kami tidak punya pengalaman dan tidak ada tempat untuk belajar. Namun kami tetap memulai. Sejak musim gugur tahun lalu kami rutin turun ke jalan membagikan makanan. Awalnya kami banyak belajar dari kesalahan sendiri. Setelah setiap aksi, kami mengevaluasi apa yang perlu diperbaiki atau ditambahkan. Kini kami memiliki cukup pengalaman dan dengan senang hati membagikannya kepada siapa saja yang ingin memulai kegiatan serupa.




2. Orang-orang seperti apa yang biasanya datang kepada kalian?




Andrew: 

Sebagian besar yang kami bantu adalah para lansia yang harus bertahan hidup dengan uang pensiun yang sangat kecil. Selain itu ada juga pejalan kaki, pelajar, dan orang-orang yang tertarik dengan kegiatan kami lalu ikut makan bersama.




Oleg: 

Beragam orang datang kepada kami. Ada tunawisma, warga lanjut usia, pekerja metro, pengunjung pasar, hingga orang yang sekadar lewat. Lokasi kami berada di antara stasiun metro dan pasar, jadi banyak orang singgah.




Sebagian datang untuk makan, tetapi ada juga yang ingin mengobrol, mencari tahu siapa kami, berbagi gagasan, atau menceritakan masalah yang mereka hadapi.




Kebanyakan mendukung apa yang kami lakukan, bahkan menawarkan bantuan. Namun ada juga yang bersikap negatif. Mereka percaya bahwa “orang yang tenggelam harus menyelamatkan dirinya sendiri.”




Dari mereka kami sering mendengar komentar seperti, “Kenapa kalian memberi makan mereka?”, “Kalau lapar suruh saja mereka bekerja,” atau “Kalau perang terjadi, siapa yang akan melindungi kalian?”




Kami mencoba menjelaskan bahwa tidak ada masalah yang benar-benar hanya milik orang lain. Kami juga berusaha menjelaskan akar penyebab perang dan pentingnya solidaritas serta saling mendukung satu sama lain.




3. Sejauh mana warga Samara mendukung kalian?




Andrew: 

Kadang orang menghubungi kami setelah menerima selebaran yang kami bagikan. Sebagian menghubungi lewat media sosial dan menyumbangkan bahan makanan, sementara yang lain memberikan bantuan dana.




Oleg: 

Seperti yang sudah saya katakan, sebagian besar orang yang datang mendukung gagasan kami. Banyak yang menawarkan bantuan.




Gerakan ini juga cukup menarik perhatian anak muda. Ada yang membantu menyebarkan informasi, ada pula yang bergabung dan menjadi anggota aktif kelompok kami.




4. Bagaimana hubungan gerakan kalian dengan vegetarianisme dan veganisme?




Andrew: 

Sebagian besar anggota kelompok kami adalah vegan dan vegetarian. Beberapa lainnya masih mengonsumsi semua jenis makanan. Namun dalam setiap kegiatan kami hanya menyajikan makanan vegan.




Oleg: 

Pertama-tama perlu dijelaskan bahwa vegetarianisme dan veganisme adalah dua hal yang berbeda.




Vegetarian tidak mengonsumsi daging, umumnya karena mereka tidak ingin memakan tubuh hewan yang dibunuh manusia. Vegan tidak hanya menghindari daging, tetapi juga semua produk yang berasal dari hewan seperti susu, telur, dan keju, karena mereka menolak segala bentuk eksploitasi terhadap hewan.




Salah satu prinsip utama gerakan ini adalah non-kekerasan, yaitu menolak segala bentuk kekerasan yang dilakukan manusia. Perang adalah contoh kekerasan manusia terhadap sesamanya. Eksploitasi dalam bentuk apa pun juga merupakan kekerasan. Kemiskinan sendiri adalah akibat dari eksploitasi orang biasa oleh mereka yang kaya.




Eksploitasi terhadap hewan juga merupakan bentuk kekerasan. Karena itulah kami tidak menggunakan produk hewani dalam kegiatan kami.




Namun menjadi vegan bukan syarat untuk bergabung dengan Food Not Bombs. Memaksa seseorang berhenti mengonsumsi produk hewani juga bertentangan dengan prinsip kami. Itu adalah pilihan pribadi masing-masing individu. Di kelompok kami ada vegan dan ada pula yang tidak, tetapi hal itu tidak pernah menjadi sumber konflik.




5. Seberapa penting solidaritas dan gotong royong di bawah negara yang otoriter?




Andrew: 

Solidaritas dan gotong royong adalah dua hal yang dapat digunakan masyarakat untuk menghadapi tekanan dari negara.




Oleg: 

Solidaritas dan gotong royong penting dalam kondisi apa pun, bukan hanya di negara otoriter.




Setiap orang adalah bagian dari masyarakat dan karena itu bergantung pada masyarakat serta orang-orang di sekitarnya. Ketika kita membiarkan seseorang menghadapi masalahnya sendirian, kita turut membiarkan masalah itu menyebar. Pada akhirnya masalah tersebut bisa menimpa siapa saja, termasuk diri kita sendiri.




Karena itulah kami berusaha memperhatikan siapa pun yang membutuhkan uluran tangan.




6. Menurut kalian, mana yang lebih buruk, kemiskinan atau perang?




Andrew: 

Sulit mengatakan mana yang lebih buruk. Selama kapitalisme masih ada, orang miskin akan terus dimiskinkan dan banyak yang mati karena kelaparan. Sementara kelas penguasa di berbagai negara akan terus mengadu domba masyarakat agar saling membunuh demi kepentingan elite dalam perang.




Oleg: 

Sulit menjawabnya karena keduanya saling berkaitan.




Kemiskinan sering kali merupakan akibat dari perang. Karena perang, banyak orang kehilangan nyawa, keluarga, sahabat, dan orang-orang yang mereka cintai.




Sementara itu, orang-orang kaya justru mendapatkan keuntungan terbesar dari perang. Mereka tidak mempertaruhkan nyawa, kesehatan, atau rumah mereka sendiri. Mereka dapat dengan tenang menentukan nasib ribuan bahkan jutaan orang lain.




Dan sering kali, para tentara yang pulang dari perang justru berakhir miskin dan terabaikan. Jadi bagi saya, perang dan kemiskinan adalah dua hal yang tidak bisa dipisahkan.




7. Jika tidak rahasia, apa rencana gerakan ini ke depan?




Andrew: 

Kami berencana membuka titik distribusi makanan kedua di kawasan lain yang juga memiliki banyak warga membutuhkan.




Kami juga memiliki berbagai gagasan untuk proyek sosial dan lingkungan lainnya. Sayangnya, saat ini kami belum memiliki cukup waktu dan tenaga untuk mewujudkannya.




Oleg: 

Dalam waktu dekat kami ingin mulai membagikan makanan di dua lokasi sekaligus agar bisa menjangkau lebih banyak orang.




Kami juga ingin lebih aktif menyebarkan informasi tentang gerakan ini dan gagasan-gagasannya, sehingga kelompok-kelompok independen serupa dapat tumbuh di kota-kota lain.




Kami terus berusaha berkembang, menetapkan tujuan baru, dan mewujudkannya satu per satu.

Nonviolent Citizen Resistance Moves the World Social Forum Forward in Benin

The session brings together activists and scholars from different traditions who exchange perspectives on the ecological crisis, peace, democracy, and social justice, while exploring the wisdom resources that inspire their movements. It examines whether today’s environmental, political, and social crises reflect a deeper civilizational crisis, and discusses pathways toward ecological justice, peace, and a more sustainable future.

Standing with Sudan: Humanitarian action and global advocacy:

The session explores how civil society, humanitarian organizations, grassroots movements, and international networks are responding to the ongoing crisis in Sudan, and how they can work further through coordinated action and solidarity. title: Ex-Oil Engineer Turned Climate Whistleblower: We Face Collapse.
content:
The summer of 2026 will go down in history books as the hottest, driest and most deadly set of heatwaves Britain has ever experienced. This weather isn’t normal – but it is predictable according to a global consensus of scientists. And yet this summer, according to the science, will be one of the coolest summers we ever have again. Things will only get hotter from here.

Beginning his career as an oil-rig engineer before retraining as a climate scientist, Kevin Anderson’s career has been an extraordinary journey. On Downstream this week, Aaron Bastani sat down with him to discuss what has become his life’s work: sounding the alarm on man-made climate change, and on the fossil fuel industry that gave him his start.

Just how much has the planet heated, and why? Is the Paris Agreement’s aim of keeping heating to beneath 1.5°C still achievable, or delusional cope? What are the political obstacles to tackling the issue? Having worked with Andy Burnham in Manchester, what does Kevin think he will do on climate, as PM? Is avoiding catastrophe still possible, and if so, how much time have we got to act, before it’s too late?

title: Letter from the mudflats Hai-Dang Phan
content:
Mud envelopes my feet, dark and cool, slick with sea. It’s low tide, and the sea has receded to reveal a massive mudflat stretching as far as the eye can see. We are at Tân Thành beach, roughly two hours by car from Saigon, on the coast of Vietnam’s Mekong Delta. It is early January—the dry season in the tropical south—when huge numbers of migratory shorebirds can be found on this expanse. Following the lead of our guide, Ba and I cautiously navigate the ankle-deep water of a tidal channel. From atop the sea wall a storm-grey heron watches our slow progress. To the north and east, fishing huts perch high on bamboo posts. To the south, giant steel transmission towers dominate the horizon as they march offshore towards rows of wind turbines. On the muddy backshore, fishing boats lie stranded with nowhere to go, outsized eyes painted on their fading prows. They are the same kind of boats that my family used when we fled the country over forty years ago. We are sloshing across the mudflats this morning because somewhere out there might be a spoon-billed sandpiper, one of the world’s rarest shorebirds and a critically endangered species. A few regular, if elusive, birds are recorded every winter here at Tân Thành. Our guide is Bùi Thành Trung—or, as he prefers it, Toby. He’s one the best birders in Vietnam, a shorebird specialist with a knack for finding “spoonies”, as he affectionately calls them. “Stay inside the channel!” Toby shouts, spotting scope balanced over a shoulder. We have about two hours before the tide makes it too dangerous to be wandering the mudflats. We aren’t the only ones making the most of low tide. Further out, dozens of local women are digging for clams. The watery path leads to the first set of makeshift bamboo “monkey bridges” we’ll need to cross. My seventy-four-year-old father stops in his tracks, considers the 30-metre obstacle course, his old knees, his bad balance, and tells us “kids” to go ahead without him. But Toby has just the pep talk. “You’re still cứng” he says, clenching his fist and smiling—still hard, still tough. That’s all it takes; Ba comes along. There is something simultaneously exhilarating and comforting about being at Tân Thành. There’s no point bothering with footwear because they’ll only get stuck in the mud. Earlier, the act of taking off our shoes before setting foot on the mudflat called to mind the familiar Asian custom before entering a home. We are, after all, guests here in what Toby calls “Spoonyland”. For the past few days, Ba and I have been on a meandering road trip through the Mekong Delta, from Saigon to the river town of Châu Đốc near Cambodia. He wanted to show me some of the places where he was stationed and fought during the war, some fifty years ago, as an officer of a patrol boat unit in the South Vietnamese Navy. Today, we return to our primary mission: to experience Vietnam through its birds. Whenever we returned to Vietnam in the past, we usually spent all our time visiting family. For once, I wanted to see the country itself. On this matter, Ba and I found common ground. While he’s no avid birdwatcher like me, Ba likes a good challenge and wants to see as much of Vietnam as he still can. Given the country’s long, distinctive coastline, a trip focused on shorebirds seemed essential, and searching for the spoon-billed sandpiper offered us a chance to do something extraordinary: witness a bird brought back from the brink of extinction. The guide I initially contacted was unavailable, but put me in touch with his friend, Toby. I knew about Toby from eBird, an online platform that birdwatchers the world over use to record and share sightings. Toby was the top “lister” in Vietnam, with 750 species observed—a distinction that filled me with unexpected pride when I first saw his Vietnamese name on top of a leaderboard stacked with Anglo-sounding names. Toby studied business administration and held a decent desk job for an industrial sales company. Then, one day, a brief encounter with a sunbird ignited his passion for birds. More than ten years later, Toby has explored nearly every province in Vietnam on a quest to photograph every bird species in the country. Reaching the sandbar peninsula, we catch our first glimpse of the shorebirds. I can’t make most of them out; they are only shapes flying back and forth. The birds are everywhere, in disorienting abundance, in wondrous array. How the hell are we going to find a tiny “spoonie”—a bird the weight of a lightbulb and the length of a compact smartphone—amid these thronging masses? Toby quickly sets up the tripod and scope, and begins scanning through the active groups of small sandpipers. He makes it look easy, but I know Toby has logged countless observation hours in the field. It was here at Tân Thành, he tells me, where he developed a passion for shorebirds. He owes much to his birding mentor, Nguyễn Hoài Bảo, an ornithology instructor at Vietnam National University and a renowned bird ecologist in Southeast Asia. Working methodically, Toby shares some tips. Forget about looking for the spoon-shaped bill. Focus on behaviour: look for the most active shorebird, the one with its head down, swishing its bill side-to-side. Another clue is habitat: spoonbills prefer mixed sandy tidal mudflats with uneven surfaces and very shallow water. Look for the tiny little puddles, the ones that are just barely pools. That’s what the spoonies like. Last night, like a bad student cramming before an exam, I studied up on the spoon-billed sandpiper on Google. Their namesake bill can also look like a tiny black shovel or soft harpoon. During their summer on the coastal tundra, a vibrant reddish brown color wash spreads across their faces, breast, and back. These months on their wintering grounds, they turn a paler grey, clean white as smooth seashells underneath. Just over a decade ago, the spoon-billed sandpiper was on the brink of extinction, their global population plummeting to an estimated 100 breeding pairs in 2011. Ongoing international conservation efforts are slowing steep population declines caused by habitat loss, illegal trapping, and climate change. But they still remain critically endangered. Before the idea of this trip took hold, I didn’t even know this bird existed. Now, I’m searching for this rare thing on the dull edge of extinction, as if it might show me a way back to a country I might have called my homeland, had life not taken us altogether elsewhere. Fucking hell!” Toby shouts, his face still buried in the scope. “I found the spoonie!” He adjusts the focus and steps aside. I peer through the scope with an anticipatory thrill. At first, there’s just a little cloud of feathers. Slowly, the bird takes shape: white-and-grey tear-shaped body, black legs like two black twigs. Tail up, head down, beak busy. I think I can make out a tiny black spoon of a bill but honestly can’t be sure. Ba looks next. I provide unsolicited commentary about its near extinction. He’s visibly struggling with the scope. Does he see the spoonie? “Well, I definitely see a bird,” Ba says, chuckling. Then something spooks the shorebirds. All at once, they fly off as if a great wind has blown them away. “Oh no! There they go,” I say despairingly. “They’re leaving!” A little rush of sorrow. I’m not ready to say goodbye. “You will see, they will go out, they will come back,” Toby replies reassuringly. “They fly, make a round, and they will come back.” Come,” Toby says in English, “I will show you new species.” He proceeds to lead me across the mudflat, pointing out every kind of shorebird present. Black-bellied plover. White-faced plover. Red-necked stint. Common greenshank. Terek sandpiper. Marsh sandpiper. Curlew sandpiper. We walk in the stop-and-start rhythm of birders, pausing in front of many groups of birds, keeping a respectful distance. Meanwhile, Ba hangs back with Toby’s assistant, Ngan, absorbed with a group of impressive Eurasian curlew. “I will show you new species” becomes a refrain, as if Toby is naming creation. Far Eastern curlew. Great knot. Bar-tailed godwit. I know Toby is just doing his job, adding to the morning’s tally of species seen. Yet I also get the strong sense that he wants to show me the rich avian diversity and abundance at Tân Thành, and the ecological significance of these intertidal flats. I can’t help hearing in Toby’s voice the sound of ecological worry, too. I have read the reports. I know shorebirds worldwide are experiencing steep, alarming declines throughout their range, with many species losing more than 50 per cent of their population over the last three decades. To assess the present status and distribution of the spoon-billed sandpiper in Vietnam, an international team—led by Nguyễn Hoài Bảo and including Toby—conducted a dozen shorebird count surveys between September 2019 and March 2020. The group’s 2023 research paper identified Tân Thành as the most important wintering ground for the spoon-billed sandpiper in Vietnam, along with supporting many other threatened waterbird species on the East Asian–Australasian Flyway, one of the most significant migratory bird paths in the world. The team also discovered a few previously unknown wintering sites, and found evidence of habitat loss and the rampant use of mist nets. Though Vietnam boasts an extensive coastline, few coastal wetland sites have been identified to support migratory shorebirds. A crucial stopover on the flyway, Tân Thành beach still lacks formal, strictly enforced legal protections. The researchers’ report underscores the urgent need to designate new protected areas for migratory birds in the Mekong Delta, so as to avoid losing precious wetland habitats like mangrove forests, salt marshes, and intertidal mudflats to poorly planned coastal development projects. Will the spoon-billed sandpiper survive us and our twenty-first-century world? Conservationists are doing everything they can to make the answer “yes”. Another spoonie! As I am checking in with Ba, who has been photographing a cooperative group of big Caspian terns parked on the flats, Toby scopes another spoon-billed sandpiper. Even more remarkable: this spoonie is leg-flagged. Flags and bands, carrying unique alpha-numeric codes, have long been used by conservation biologists to study the movements, behaviour, and survival of birds. The bird is too far away, and too active, for Toby to make out the letters on the flag. He’ll need to obtain a documentary photo. Since Toby left his camera back at the hotel in Gò Công, Ba happily hands his over. Toby crabwalks 10, 20 yards towards the target spoonie. I try to follow, but my knees give out and I nearly faceplant in the mud, which makes Ba and Ngan laugh. After a few attempts, Toby looks back and gives us a thumbs-up. We huddle and stare at images of a small, white-and-grey shorebird foraging the mudflat. I can clearly see the sandpiper’s spatulate bill: it looks like a tiny ice cream spoon sticking out of its little face. Toby recites the letters on the leg-flag aloud: “H-O”. The slightly stunned expression on his face is hard to read. Ba looks pleasantly shocked. “Really? ‘H-O’?” I know what he is thinking. We haven’t learnt anything yet about the bird’s life history, but to us, and many others in the Vietnamese diaspora, “H-O” stands for “Humanitarian Operation”, immediately calling to mind the HO immigration programmes of the 1980s and 1990s that resettled former South Vietnamese political detainees and their families to the US. My family did not come to the US through the HO programme. Ba would have qualified, given the four years he spent after the war in “re-education” camps, but the HO process could take years. Instead, in late December of 1981, we became those who “vượt biên”—fleeing the country on the same kind of fishing boats we saw stranded on the backshore. I don’t know what Ba makes of these converging lines of flight: our escape from Vietnam as political refugees over forty years, and our return to the country as birdwatching ecotourists. He simply smiles his toothy smile while I ponder signs and omens. It doesn’t take long before someone associated with the Spoon-billed Sandpiper Task Force responds to Toby’s post on Facebook. Here’s what we learn: SBS White HO came out of a breeding programme where conservationists in northeast Russia collect eggs, hatch them in captivity, and hand-rear chicks before releasing them back into the wild. SBS White HO hatched on 7 July 2021, the offspring of two other tagged sandpipers, White 1H and Lime 88; two weeks later, on 26 July, SBS White HO was released around Meynypilgyno. These facts help me see the spoonbill as an individual with a specific life history. I imagine his summers amid the flowering meadows and ponds of the tundra, his migration flight, his mornings on the mudflats at Tân Thành. It’s actually the third time Toby has crossed paths with SBS White HO, and the second for Ngan. Their first time had been in December 2021, when they were conducting an environmental impact report on the Tân Phú Đông Offshore Wind Farm, whose towers and turbines are now fixtures in the landscape. Toby’s second time was a year later, while leading a private birding tour. He hadn’t seen SBS White HO in 2023, nor had there been any reported sightings on eBird. Had the bird succumbed from exhaustion during its 8,000-kilometre journey? Had it dropped out of the sky, or been caught in a farmer’s net? Or had it decided to follow other spoon-billed sandpipers, a significant number of whom could be found wintering in coastal Myanmar and Bangladesh? But here SBS White HO was again. I venture a question for Toby in my broken Vietnamese: “And how do you feel seeing this spoonie again here this morning?” “I feel đầy hy vọng,” Toby says, and asks what that means in English. “Hopeful,” I answer. Toby repeats it after me: hope-full. A quicksilver band of blue thickens the horizon line, the tide coming in. Ngan whispers something in Vietnamese to Toby, who then says, “We go now.” But we all stay where we are, our feet planted in the mud. I take a parting look through the scope. He’s still there, a cloudy puff of feathers wrestling a tiny crab, and I feel what Toby felt—đầy hy vọng, as if discovering a new species of hope. contentBlocks.text: Mud envelopes my feet, dark and cool, slick with sea. It’s low tide, and the sea has receded to reveal a massive mudflat stretching as far as the eye can see. We are at Tân Thành beach, roughly two hours by car from Saigon, on the coast of Vietnam’s Mekong Delta. It is early January—the dry season in the tropical south—when huge numbers of migratory shorebirds can be found on this expanse.

Following the lead of our guide, Ba and I cautiously navigate the ankle-deep water of a tidal channel. From atop the sea wall a storm-grey heron watches our slow progress. To the north and east, fishing huts perch high on bamboo posts. To the south, giant steel transmission towers dominate the horizon as they march offshore towards rows of wind turbines. On the muddy backshore, fishing boats lie stranded with nowhere to go, outsized eyes painted on their fading prows. They are the same kind of boats that my family used when we fled the country over forty years ago.

We are sloshing across the mudflats this morning because somewhere out there might be a spoon-billed sandpiper, one of the world’s rarest shorebirds and a critically endangered species. A few regular, if elusive, birds are recorded every winter here at Tân Thành. Our guide is Bùi Thành Trung—or, as he prefers it, Toby. He’s one the best birders in Vietnam, a shorebird specialist with a knack for finding “spoonies”, as he affectionately calls them.

“Stay inside the channel!” Toby shouts, spotting scope balanced over a shoulder. We have about two hours before the tide makes it too dangerous to be wandering the mudflats. We aren’t the only ones making the most of low tide. Further out, dozens of local women are digging for clams.

The watery path leads to the first set of makeshift bamboo “monkey bridges” we’ll need to cross. My seventy-four-year-old father stops in his tracks, considers the 30-metre obstacle course, his old knees, his bad balance, and tells us “kids” to go ahead without him. But Toby has just the pep talk. “You’re still cứng” he says, clenching his fist and smiling—still hard, still tough. That’s all it takes; Ba comes along.

There is something simultaneously exhilarating and comforting about being at Tân Thành. There’s no point bothering with footwear because they’ll only get stuck in the mud. Earlier, the act of taking off our shoes before setting foot on the mudflat called to mind the familiar Asian custom before entering a home. We are, after all, guests here in what Toby calls “Spoonyland”.

For the past few days, Ba and I have been on a meandering road trip through the Mekong Delta, from Saigon to the river town of Châu Đốc near Cambodia. He wanted to show me some of the places where he was stationed and fought during the war, some fifty years ago, as an officer of a patrol boat unit in the South Vietnamese Navy.

For once, I wanted to see the country itself. On this matter, Ba and I found common ground. While he’s no avid birdwatcher like me, Ba likes a good challenge and wants to see as much of Vietnam as he still can.

Given the country’s long, distinctive coastline, a trip focused on shorebirds seemed essential, and searching for the spoon-billed sandpiper offered us a chance to do something extraordinary: witness a bird brought back from the brink of extinction. The guide I initially contacted was unavailable, but put me in touch with his friend, Toby. I knew about Toby from eBird, an online platform that birdwatchers the world over use to record and share sightings. Toby was the top “lister” in Vietnam, with 750 species observed—a distinction that filled me with unexpected pride when I first saw his Vietnamese name on top of a leaderboard stacked with Anglo-sounding names.

Toby studied business administration and held a decent desk job for an industrial sales company. Then, one day, a brief encounter with a sunbird ignited his passion for birds. More than ten years later, Toby has explored nearly every province in Vietnam on a quest to photograph every bird species in the country.

Reaching the sandbar peninsula, we catch our first glimpse of the shorebirds. I can’t make most of them out; they are only shapes flying back and forth. The birds are everywhere, in disorienting abundance, in wondrous array. How the hell are we going to find a tiny “spoonie”—a bird the weight of a lightbulb and the length of a compact smartphone—amid these thronging masses?

Toby quickly sets up the tripod and scope, and begins scanning through the active groups of small sandpipers. He makes it look easy, but I know Toby has logged countless observation hours in the field. It was here at Tân Thành, he tells me, where he developed a passion for shorebirds. He owes much to his birding mentor, Nguyễn Hoài Bảo, an ornithology instructor at Vietnam National University and a renowned bird ecologist in Southeast Asia.

Working methodically, Toby shares some tips. Forget about looking for the spoon-shaped bill. Focus on behaviour: look for the most active shorebird, the one with its head down, swishing its bill side-to-side. Another clue is habitat: spoonbills prefer mixed sandy tidal mudflats with uneven surfaces and very shallow water. Look for the tiny little puddles, the ones that are just barely pools. That’s what the spoonies like.

Last night, like a bad student cramming before an exam, I studied up on the spoon-billed sandpiper on Google. Their namesake bill can also look like a tiny black shovel or soft harpoon. During their summer on the coastal tundra, a vibrant reddish brown color wash spreads across their faces, breast, and back. These months on their wintering grounds, they turn a paler grey, clean white as smooth seashells underneath.

Just over a decade ago, the spoon-billed sandpiper was on the brink of extinction, their global population plummeting to an estimated 100 breeding pairs in 2011. Ongoing international conservation efforts are slowing steep population declines caused by habitat loss, illegal trapping, and climate change. But they still remain critically endangered.

Will the spoon-billed sandpiper survive us and our twenty-first-century world? Conservationists are doing everything they can to make the answer “yes”.

Flags and bands, carrying unique alpha-numeric codes, have long been used by conservation biologists to study the movements, behaviour, and survival of birds. The bird is too far away, and too active, for Toby to make out the letters on the flag. He’ll need to obtain a documentary photo.

Since Toby left his camera back at the hotel in Gò Công, Ba happily hands his over. Toby crabwalks 10, 20 yards towards the target spoonie. I try to follow, but my knees give out and I nearly faceplant in the mud, which makes Ba and Ngan laugh. After a few attempts, Toby looks back and gives us a thumbs-up. I can clearly see the sandpiper’s spatulate bill: it looks like a tiny ice cream spoon sticking out of its little face. Toby recites the letters on the leg-flag aloud: “H-O”. The slightly stunned expression on his face is hard to read.

title: "Fire Climate": Hot, Dry, Windy Days Are Becoming Common, Making Wildfires Harder to Control
content:
The Pacific Northwest is facing its worst fire season in more than 30 years. Scientists say drought, extreme heat and climate change are making wildfire seasons longer, more frequent and more destructive across the western United States.

“The homes, the communities, they’re just not simply prepared for fire,” says Paul Hessburg, former senior research ecologist at the U.S. Forest Service and professor of fire and landscape ecology at the University of Washington. Hessburg walks us through the history of the region, from the controlled fires practiced by Indigenous peoples before European settlement to present-day ecologically unsound factors including “accidental ignitions, dense forests, the wrong kinds of fuels on the ground [and] rapidly changing climate.”

title: A controversial plan to update Line 5 just suffered a major loss at the Michigan Supreme Court
content:
In a win for opponents of Enbridge Energy’s Line 5 pipeline, the Michigan Supreme Court vacated a key permit last week for a proposed project that would replace a segment of the pipeline running underneath an environmentally-sensitive area of the Great Lakes, finding that a state commission did not examine the full scope of possible harm to the environment.

Following the 6-1 decision, the justices remanded the permit back to the Michigan Public Service Commission for a more thorough review, which likely extends the timeline for a decision on a project that’s already been mired in legal and procedural hurdles for years.

Enbridge Energy received the permit in 2023 for its proposal to replace a segment of the oil and natural gas liquids pipeline — which connects lakes Michigan and Huron via the Straits of Mackinac — with a new one encased in a tunnel buried in the lakebed. Environmental groups and tribal nations appealed the decision, landing the case before the state’s highest court this year.

Writing for a nearly unanimous court in a 58-page opinion , Justice Elizabeth Welch said that the commission didn’t consider the full range of potential environmental harms, nor did it look at how the project would impact the public’s right to use the state’s natural resources, which includes the Great Lakes — protections granted under the state’s public trust doctrine.

“We cannot fault (the commission) for this failure, because there was little authority on this issue prior to our decision today. Even so, it was error,” the opinion stated.

Justices found that the commission incorrectly limited its scope of review under the Michigan Environmental Protection Act to just the tunnel, when it should have examined how the project would impact the broader pipeline. Line 5 transports crude oil and natural gas liquids 645 miles from Superior, Wisconsin, through Michigan to Sarnia, Ontario, with 4.5 miles of the pipeline crossing the straits.

In its new review, the justices said that the public service commission must answer whether the tunnel project will extend the lifespan of the 73-year-old pipeline, and if it does, determine what impacts there are to the environment and to the public trust.

“It is impossible to prevent or mitigate an environmental risk without understanding the nature of that risk,” the justices wrote.

Lawyers for the plaintiffs — four tribal nations across Michigan and three environmental groups — argued that because the tunnel project would extend the pipeline’s lifespan, it causes harm by increasing the risk of oil spills along Line 5’s entirety and increased greenhouse gas emissions from the fossil fuels it transports.

“The court has made clear that our understanding of environmental harm, it’s a practical understanding, but it’s also a broad one,” said Chad Hughes, senior attorney for the Environmental Law & Policy Center, which argued with the plaintiffs. “There’s no requirement to narrowly focus on the physical location of the project. You look at the environmental harms where they happen.”

By broadening the scope of reviews under the Michigan Environmental Protection Act, opponents said conversations about shutting down the entire pipeline are finally a possibility. The justices wrote that “a meaningful examination” of alternatives can’t happen until the commission determines the full impacts of the project.

“The door has been kicked open to an imaginable future where we can talk about alternatives other than Line 5,” said President Whitney Gravelle of the Bay Mills Indian Community, one of the plaintiffs in the case.

In a statement, Enbridge spokesperson Ryan Duffy wrote that the company disagrees and is disappointed by the ruling, calling it an additional delay to a project that has already been under review for nearly a decade. Enbridge is reviewing the opinion and assessing legal options, he said.

“What remains unchanged is our commitment to operating Line 5 safely and responsibly, incorporating enhanced safety measures in the Straits, and protecting Michigan’s natural resources for generations to come,” the statement said.

The lone dissenting opinion from Justice Brian Zahra said that the court’s directive to consider the full scope of potential harms was “a moral hazard,” because state regulators already decided Line 5 was in the public interest when it approved construction more than 70 years ago.

But Zahra agreed with the majority on the requirement to consider the public trust doctrine, and recommended that the commission use last month’s permit issuance from a separate state agency as a guide. The Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy said the necessity of the tunnel in preventing an oil spill in the Great Lakes outweighed other public interests.

Separate from the tunnel project, Line 5 faces legal challenges from groups that have fought to shut down the pipeline for years, including Governor Gretchen Whitmer’s administration. This spring, a unanimous ruling from the U.S. Supreme Court paved the way for state court proceedings on whether the aging pipeline can continue operating in the straits.

Last week’s ruling was also a significant win for public trust considerations, according to environmental lawyers. The public service commission declined to consider the public trust doctrine in its analysis prior to issuing its permit in 2023, a decision upheld by the Michigan Court of Appeals because it argued the commission “possesses only that authority bestowed upon it by statute.”

The justices reversed this ruling, agreeing in a concurrent case with plaintiff Flow Water Advocates that the state legislature grants the public service commission “the authority — and indeed, the responsibility — to consider the public trust doctrine.”

“It is elevating the rights of the public. It’s saying that the intergenerational equity that we promise our children will be there,” said Liz Kirkwood, executive director of Flow.

Gravelle with the Bay Mills Indian Community said this new consideration of the doctrine is a win for tribal treaty rights. Tribes in Michigan have long asserted that Line 5’s operation interferes with their rights to fight, hunt, and gather on treaty-ceded lands, which include the Straits of Mackinac.

“You can’t have a treaty right to fish if you don’t have healthy waterways for fish to spawn. You can’t have a treaty right to hunt if you’re cutting down forests and filling wetlands, you can’t have a treaty right to gather if you’re polluting waterways and watersheds that are impacting plant species that you rely on for ceremonial or medicinal purposes,” she said.

The court’s ruling reflects an Indigenous way of thinking that could shape future environmental reviews, Gravelle said.

“We have teachings in our culture that require us to think generations ahead: Is the decision I made today going to benefit seven generations from now?” she said. “We need more holistic, proactive decision-making from our state agencies moving forward. And so, I hope that’s the pathway carved.”

title: How creativity — and children — have kept Albania’s revolution alive
content:
This article How creativity — and children — have kept Albania’s revolution alive was originally published by Waging Nonviolence .

It was on the third day of the revolution that the mood changed. Once again, many thousands of Albanians had descended on Tirana’s central square after work. Once again, the speeches and banners were focused on stopping a wild and legally protected coastline from being razed for a luxury resort. But this time the vibe was tense. Some people had entered the crowd who were angry, screaming abuses and trying to set fire to the placards.

Ilir Kaso, an artist and lecturer at Tirana University of Arts, stood nearby with his two daughters, aged 11 and seven. “My daughters were very frightened. My youngest asked to leave the protest, and so we did,” recalled Kaso. But as they emerged from the crowd, they found themselves facing what Kaso describes as “the flamingo group,” a collection of a hundred or so protesters wielding pink flamingo banners and a few pink polystyrene flamingos on poles. “‘Papa look, flamingos, let’s go there,’ said my youngest, and immediately I understood what we had to do.”

The flamingo group was a loose coalition of artists and environmental activists based in Tirana. The partnership had first formed more than a decade earlier under the banner of “Friends of Vjosa,” a movement to stop one of Europe’s last wild rivers from being splintered by 45 hydroelectric dams. Kaso became a part of what proved to be a very successful campaign. It birthed Europe’s first Wild River National Park, and on a personal level, it transformed Kaso’s art, pulling him away from abstraction and towards nature. He and his wife named their first daughter after the river.

When trucks and bulldozers suddenly rolled into a protected part of the river’s delta in late April, and started fencing off a large section of the coastline, the coalition quickly remobilized, meeting in person and via WhatsApp groups to work out how to stop the destruction. Kaso attended the first small protests along the fence line, photographing the flattening of ancient sand dunes where turtles nested, and the laying of concrete over wetlands that host hundreds of migratory bird species, many of them endangered.

Kaso had followed but not posted in the WhatsApp debate over which bird should be the symbol of their campaign. The environmental activists wanted one of the more threatened species to be made prominent — the Dalmatian pelican, the Northern lapwing — but the artists had decided on the flamingo, an easily recognizable bird with an iconic color and shape. After seeing how the bird had become a refuge for his frightened children, Kaso quickly started tapping out a message in the chat.

“I wrote about what happened and how we could create somewhere stationary, a shelter where we flamingos can stay all together and bring in the children, to protect them but also to expand the good vibes,” he said. “Because children have such good energy, they don’t have doubts or traumas like us. And we cannot wait for this protest to be damaged and become violent. This bad energy is going to destroy everything. We have to fight this with good energy, but by going out of the crowd.”

Kaso had experience setting up a shelter like this. During the pandemic he had helped to open and run a community school for his daughters and other young children in his area. The experience had a profound effect on how he taught his art students. After the pandemic, he rejected rigid lesson plans and formulas to be more curious and open to their ideas. “The children taught me a lot,” he said with a smile.

The artists and activists in the WhatsApp chat immediately embraced Kaso’s idea. Not only was there a shared fear of violence derailing this uprising, but the surging size of the crowds was clearly straining families. Every evening, between the speeches on the square, messages were going out over the microphone about lost children who needed to be found. On the chat, artists started offering to bring coloring pens and run drawing sessions. The next day, 20 feet of paper was laid out beside the Pyramid of Tirana, a tree-lined landmark between the square where protesters gathered and the prime minister’s office that they marched to. It was instantly flooded with grateful parents and curious children.

The Children’s Corner, as it is now called, has become an established feature of the revolution, entertaining children for approximately three hours every evening. On busy days, more than a hundred children will sit on the ground drawing their favorite birds, singing into megaphones, or playing with flamingo placards, while a dozen adults strive to monitor activities. It has become a hub not just for families but the flamingo group itself, who use the space to synchronize their chants, strategize about their movements, and pass out their pink foam placards to fellow revolutionaries.

Kaso describes the Children’s Corner as the sun of the protest, always radiating with light, fun and good vibes. And the flamingo group has taken on the role of dispersing those vibes to the rest of the protest. When a speech has been particularly aggressive or divisive, a flamingo parade will take flight, weaving into the crowd, and then chanting, drumming and dancing to relieve the tension. Then they will return to the Children’s Corner to recharge.

“The Children’s Corner is very important for keeping this protest peaceful,” Kaso said. “I think it is our most important weapon, like a Trojan horse, against the people who want to end this protest and make it a mess. It means the police cannot throw their gas and create aggressive situations. Also for the people — we are telling them we are here with our children and our families, so we have to be careful.”

The space has triggered an outpouring of generous donations, though much has had to be turned away. Food from strangers was considered too risky, while taking money might give the impression this was a commercial childcare service. But offers of more coloring pens and art materials have always been readily accepted.

Not everyone has welcomed the corner though. Some have accused it of diluting the revolution, of reducing it to a kind of theater, while nationalist groups have taken exception to anything connected to the flamingos, screaming “we are eagles!” (Albania is literally called “land of the eagles” in Albanian, and its flag features a double-headed black eagle.) On particularly busy days, Kaso and other volunteers have had to form human chains to stop the surging crowds from accidentally trampling the children. But each time there has been a confrontation or danger, the corner community of flamingos and parents have collectively stepped in to diffuse it.

After some 60 days of continuous protest, featuring many hundreds of thousands of Albanians packed within a few square blocks, there has been remarkably little violence. Some eggs were thrown at the cars of politicians as they entered the nearby parliament building, and some windows were broken at a local police station after six egg-throwers were pepper-sprayed, arrested and held there before being released.

With the help of art materials and studio space from NGOs and private donors, many hundreds of pink foam flamingo banners have been produced and handed out. In the city, they’ve started to function like a pride flag, a marker stuck outside bars and cafés to show solidarity with the revolution. “Most of the time we connect revolution to war and destruction and going back,” Kaso said, “but this is a big lesson for us about how we can think about a revolution. And the children are the most important part to teach us this.”

Corporate aggression backfires

Besjana Guri is tired. She started our interview by getting a date wrong by a decade and then laughing. The environmental activist has attended every day of the revolution so far, using a projector to screen rousing flamingo-themed videos on the wall of the prime minister’s office. “If you ever think of not going once, you feel you are betraying the protest. You have to go,” she said.

Guri co-led the award-winning campaign that turned the river Vjosa into a national park, and a year ago she founded Lumi (which means river in Albanian), a small organization focused on empowering women and children to protect their local environment. Two days before the Vjosa’s delta was turned into a construction site, Guri had been meeting with women in the nearby village of Zvërnec to discuss the threat to the region and organize a response.

The delta region where the Vjosa River meets the Adriatic Sea is mesmerizingly beautiful — a delicate tapestry of salt marshes, lagoons and forests. Known as Vjosa-Narta, the government awarded the coastal area full protection status in 2017. But over the last decade, as Prime Minister Edi Rama has cemented his grip over Albania’s politics, that protection has been stripped back and caveated to the point of being meaningless.

In 2018, Vjosa-Narta’s protected status was downgraded to allow an old military base within it to become a (still unfinished) airport. “The airport was the tip of the iceberg,” said Xhemal Xherri, a project manager at Protection and Preservation of Natural Environment in Albania, or PPNEA . “We always knew that somehow this airport would bring resorts to the area.”

Then in 2024, the law enforcing the protection was amended to allow the government to essentially overrule it if an opportunity was lucrative enough. A month later, Jared Kushner, son-in-law of the U.S. president, shared designs on Instagram for a huge luxury development along the coastline. Then in January of this year, the villagers in Zvërnec found themselves under virtual house arrest while Ivanka Trump, Kushner’s wife, toured the area with a troupe of architects, business associates and security guards.

But when the trucks rolled into Vjosa-Narta in late April, it was still a shock. Albanian law required public consultations, an environmental assessment and various government permits to be awarded before construction could begin. The law no longer appeared to matter. Within a week, a coalition of environmental organizations had sent representatives to document the damage as access roads were crudely carved into the pristine coastline. A week after that came the first protest.

By the time Guri and a hundred other activists and villagers had converged on the vast construction site, it had been enclosed by a fence which ran right into the sea. Watching them from the other side of the fence was one elderly security guard, and a few bored police officers. The men eventually agreed to open a gate and let the protesters inspect some of the damage. “They thought we were just ecoactivists, we were harmless,” Guri remembered.

Before the protest finished, some villagers insisted on toppling over a small section of the fence — a symbol of their disgust. For them, this was not just about land destruction but land ownership. Their community had lived on this coast for generations, yet the land had been sold to Kushner by a Florida-based real estate mogul with links to cocaine-trafficking and document forgery . Some families had spent 20 years in court battling over the ownership of the land, and despite there being no legal resolution, they were suddenly being denied access to it. For now though, the fence was flimsy. It could be pushed over using body weight alone.

When the protesters returned the next Saturday, the fence and the whole mood was different. Now the barrier was concrete-based, and topped with thick curls of barbed wire. Looking through it were dozens of muscular private security guards, dressed all in black, faces obscured by sunglasses, baseball caps and masks. As the protesters marched along the fence they were shadowed by a column of police officers. “The feeling was not good,” Guri said. “It felt like there were terrorists here, people who wanted to scare and intimidate us.”

It was during the protest on the third Saturday that the intimidation turned to violence. The protesters had marched along the barrier to the beach, and with the tide low, an area of sand had been exposed that was blocked only by barbed wire. A lone villager ignored the warnings of the guards and carefully stepped over it. He was instantly pounced upon by the men in black, who wrestled him to the ground, punched him in the face and dragged him away by his arms across the beach. Another masked guard then fired pepper spray into the angry crowd, blinding both the protesters and the strangely passive line of police officers between them.

Guri was not able to attend the protest that day, but like hundreds of thousands of others, she watched a video of the assault on social media a few hours later. “Everyone that saw that moment, it was really a feeling that they were the ones being dragged,” she said, her eyes closed. Online, the video was being paired with rallying songs and nationalist poetry , and it was spreading like wildfire, well beyond the networks of activists, artists and villagers who were attending the protests. By the next day, a poster was circulating alongside it, headlined “ Albania is not for sale! ” It called for a protest in Tirana’s central square at 6 p.m. that evening.

Kaso arrived at the protest early so he could take photographs as people arrived. “I was physically trembling when I saw this huge group of people approaching,” he recalled. “It was amazing. A mix of responsibility and euphoria. A feeling that another chapter is coming. I never imagined all these years of fighting for nature and the river could be so helpful.” Guri was late, after spending her Sunday in a village outside Tirana, then hitting heavy traffic. “When I got there, I saw — I cannot count how many people. But for sure 600 people and more. I haven’t seen a bigger protest in the last 10 years for an environmental issue,” she said.

Guri was so inspired she later spoke to the crowd: “I said it took us 10 years to protect the Vjosa river and finalize the national park, but if we continue like this, we will only need 10 days to cancel this project and save the Narta.” With the speeches wrapped up, and the protest coming to an end, a chant built up among the crowd: “See you tomorrow, tomorrow more.” The template for a revolution had been set.

“The protest kept growing every day. For the first few weeks it was only growing. Not only ecoactivists but all types of people. And the majority was young people,” Guri said. “They came with banners and funny memes and interesting quotes. Then we added the element of the flamingos. That’s when the creativity began, and the creativity has really kept this protest alive.”

Building an anti-corruption revolution

Xhemal Xherri of PPNEA, along with all the activists I’ve spoken to, is adamant that the Flamingo Revolution has no leaders, that it is a spontaneous and amorphous movement featuring a patchwork of groups unified by a love of nature. The closest it comes to forming an agenda is when the crowd cheers or jeers after a speech. But PPNEA has been quietly instrumental in preparing the soil from which this revolution has bloomed, and building the relationships that could lead to its eventual success.

PPNEA was the country’s first environmental organization, established as it was transitioning away from communist dictatorship in 1991. The group took the government to court over irregularities in the airport construction contracts (the case is ongoing), and has been organizing protests against the exploitation of Vjosa-Narta for years. As Albania’s politicians were voting in the law change that meant Kushner’s luxury resorts could turn from CGI dream to reality, a hundred PPNEA activists were protesting outside parliament to condemn them.

The day before the first protest outside the construction site, for which PPNEA brought in bus-loads of Tirana-based activists, the organization invited a delegation of EU diplomats to witness the destruction firsthand. A month later, a PPNEA representative was in Strasbourg, France as the European Parliament voted in a resolution condemning the change to Albania’s law on protected areas, and making its repeal a non-negotiable condition of Albania’s accession to the EU.

Six Green members of the European Parliament then attended the protests in Tirana at the end of June, making stridently pro-revolution speeches that were adored by the crowds. Just days earlier, Prime Minister Rama had explained to a Euronews journalist how officials in his government were “fanatics of the EU faith” who would do “whatever it takes” to gain membership. The country has been seeking candidature and tirelessly negotiating its way into the bloc since 2009.

Despite this powerful endorsement from the EU, the fanatical Rama has not softened his stance on the protesters. From the beginning he has dismissed their concerns as delusional, the product of a coordinated online disinformation campaign by Iran , which he claims has simultaneously targeted both Albania and Israel as the two countries deepen their diplomatic ties .

But for Xherri, the reason social media algorithms have been promoting the Flamingo Revolution is not because of foreign interference, but simply because everybody in the capital is going to the square and posting about it. This includes many Albanian social media influencers, who have been privately requesting briefings from PPNEA on Vjosa-Narta, and amplifying the organization’s posts to new audiences.

Construction of the resort has been quietly paused, and the barbed wire fence has been removed, but so far the government has conceded nothing. Even if Rama were to repeal the law change that triggered this revolt, and consign Kushner’s project to the dustbin of history, it is unlikely to be enough to placate the people now surging through the city every evening. As the crowds have grown, so too have their demands. Today the protesters are just as likely to chant for both Rama and the leader of the opposition to be put in jail for corruption, as they are to call for nature to be protected.

Over the last few weeks, the numbers out protesting have stabilized, with a few thousand marching each week night, and the crowds ballooning again at the weekends, especially now that Albania’s sizable diaspora is returning to be a part of the revolution. The activists I talk to are all confident that the government will eventually yield, and the law will be repealed.

But when it comes to winning wider political changes, Kaso references a so far isolated incident, early in the revolution, where a group of protesters spontaneously marched out of the city and blocked a highway leading to the country’s main airport for several hours.

“The people have shown the prime minister how this protest can be escalated. Maybe one or two hundred people, which is nothing for this protest, could block the entrance of the highway which connects the city to the airport, and stay there for 24 hours, which is going to be a big loss for travel companies,” he said. “​​I don’t want to see everything escalate in a dangerous way, but if necessary we don’t only have to be creative in aesthetic ways — with posters and colors and children. We can do it in other ways.”

For now though, the flamingo group are continuing to power this protest with pink placards, good vibes and children drawing their favorite birds. And no matter what happens next, Kaso is happy. “For me the revolution has already been successful,” he said. “It’s already changed a lot. If tomorrow we are not going in the road anymore, I know very well that life in Albania is not going to be the same.”

Guri was so inspired she later spoke to the crowd: “I said it took us 10 years to protect the Vjosa river and finalize the national park, but if we continue like this, we will only need 10 days to cancel this project and save the Narta.” With the speeches wrapped up, and the protest coming to an end, a chant built up among the crowd: “See you tomorrow, tomorrow more.” The template for a revolution had been set.

And the majority was young people,” Guri said. “They came with banners and funny memes and interesting quotes. Then we added the element of the flamingos. That’s when the creativity began, and the creativity has really kept this protest alive.”
Building an anti-corruption revolution

Xhemal Xherri of PPNEA, along with all the activists I’ve spoken to, is adamant that the Flamingo Revolution has no leaders, that it is a spontaneous and amorphous movement featuring a patchwork of groups unified by a love of nature. The closest it comes to forming an agenda is when the crowd cheers or jeers after a speech. But PPNEA has been quietly instrumental in preparing the soil from which this revolution has bloomed, and building the relationships that could lead to its eventual success.

PPNEA was the country’s first environmental organization, established as it was transitioning away from communist dictatorship in 1991. The group took the government to court over irregularities in the airport construction contracts (the case is ongoing), and has been organizing protests against the exploitation of Vjosa-Narta for years. As Albania’s politicians were voting in the law change that meant Kushner’s luxury resorts could turn from CGI dream to reality, a hundred PPNEA activists were protesting outside parliament to condemn them.

The day before the first protest outside the construction site, for which PPNEA brought in bus-loads of Tirana-based activists, the organization invited a delegation of EU diplomats to witness the destruction firsthand. A month later, a PPNEA representative was in Strasbourg, France as the European Parliament voted in a resolution condemning the change to Albania’s law on protected areas, and making its repeal a non-negotiable condition of Albania’s accession to the EU.

Six Green members of the European Parliament then attended the protests in Tirana at the end of June, making stridently pro-revolution speeches that were adored by the crowds. Just days earlier, Prime Minister Rama had explained to a Euronews journalist how officials in his government were “fanatics of the EU faith” who would do “whatever it takes” to gain membership. The country has been seeking candidature and tirelessly negotiating its way into the bloc since 2009.

Despite this powerful endorsement from the EU, the fanatical Rama has not softened his stance on the protesters. From the beginning he has dismissed their concerns as delusional, the product of a coordinated online disinformation campaign by Iran , which he claims has simultaneously targeted both Albania and Israel as the two countries deepen their diplomatic ties .

But for Xherri, the reason social media algorithms have been promoting the Flamingo Revolution is not because of foreign interference, but simply because everybody in the capital is going to the square and posting about it. This includes many Albanian social media influencers, who have been privately requesting briefings from PPNEA on Vjosa-Narta, and amplifying the organization’s posts to new audiences.

contentBlocks.text: Construction of the resort has been quietly paused, and the barbed wire fence has been removed, but so far the government has conceded nothing. Even if Rama were to repeal the law change that triggered this revolt, and consign Kushner’s project to the dustbin of history, it is unlikely to be enough to placate the people now surging through the city every evening. As the crowds have grown, so too have their demands. Today the protesters are just as likely to chant for both Rama and the leader of the opposition to be put in jail for corruption, as they are to call for nature to be protected.

Over the last few weeks, the numbers out protesting have stabilized, with a few thousand marching each week night, and the crowds ballooning again at the weekends, especially now that Albania’s sizable diaspora is returning to be a part of the revolution. The activists I talk to are all confident that the government will eventually yield, and the law will be repealed.

But when it comes to winning wider political changes, Kaso references a so far isolated incident, early in the revolution, where a group of protesters spontaneously marched out of the city and blocked a highway leading to the country’s main airport for several hours.

“The people have shown the prime minister how this protest can be escalated. Maybe one or two hundred people, which is nothing for this protest, could block the entrance of the highway which connects the city to the airport, and stay there for 24 hours, which is going to be a big loss for travel companies,” he said. “​​I don’t want to see everything escalate in a dangerous way, but if necessary we don’t only have to be creative in aesthetic ways — with posters and colors and children. We can do it in other ways.”

For now though, the flamingo group are continuing to power this protest with pink placards, good vibes and children drawing their favorite birds. And no matter what happens next, Kaso is happy. “For me the revolution has already been successful,” he said. “It’s already changed a lot. If tomorrow we are not going in the road anymore, I know very well that life in Albania is not going to be the same.”

title: The bane of Murray Bookchin Thought
content:
Murray Bookchin is rightly remembered for many things. He was a self-declared anarchist for a little more than three decades; according to the hagiography written by his long-term partner he became one in the late 1950s after moving away from the Stalinism of his youth, but he didn’t become known as one under his own name until the late 60s. Plenty of other anarchists found his analyses and positions to be lacking – he abandoned class struggle in the early 70s, tried to make common cause with the nascent right-wing “anarchists” of the Libertarian Party around the same time (even speaking at one of their conventions!), offered extremely uncritical support for the Sandinistas (because their red and black flag symbolised their adherence to anarcho-syndicalism – I’m not kidding), maintained a stubbornly inexplicable adherence to a Marxoid Hegelianism, and had a love-hate relationship with electoral politics by co-founding a local chapter of the Green Party.

By the mid-1980s, many of his critics had accused him of veering away from the recognisable principles of anarchism, an allegation he studiously ignored. His bitterness at being rejected as a leading figure of American – let alone international – anarchism, of an American Left Green caucus, or as anything more than a lecturer at a small private college where he directed the Institute for Social Ecology (ISE), led him eventually to slide into increasing irrelevance. He finally quit play acting, abandoning all pretence to being an anarchist – privately by 1995 and publicly in 1999.

Among his lingering legacies for anarchists are his ecological thought outlined in The Ecology of Freedom (1982), and his attacks on anarchists who didn’t toe his particular line. The former were long surpassed by works less enamoured with industrial technology, while the latter remained unsurpassed until the publication of the unintentionally hilarious Black Flame in 2009 (in which the authors outdid Bookchin, calling him out for even accepting that his targets were anarchists at all). According to his partner Janet Biehl, Bookchin told a few people that he was taking himself out of the club at the same time he wrote Social Anarchism or Lifestyle Anarchism: An Unbridgeable Chasm . This long essay is an incoherent screed, because there is no such thing as a “lifestyle anarchist”; in it, he denounced everyone he didn’t like who still wanted to be in the club, lumping their contradictory tendencies (neo-Situationists, hedonists, individualists, adventurists, postmodernists, apolitical anti-organisationalists, pluralists, Yuppies, and other avatars of “social reaction”) into a single scapegoat meant to explain the lack of popularity of some Official Anarchism.

And once he had sown more discord than any other single Anglophone anarchist, he walked away from the debate, leaving rancour and denunciation in his wake. In its stead, he created a vulgar Hegelian hybrid of allegedly vigorous Marxist analysis and weak left-wing social democratic practise, agrarianism and urbanism, bureaucratic centralisation and “libertarian municipalism” called communalism . This idiosyncratic invention, not anarchism, is what allegedly influenced the imprisoned Marxist Öcalan to push for an improved version of Kurdish nationalism, which, naturally enough, kept plenty of room for an official leadership and a historically hierarchical party structure. Apparently, every pro-PKK/YPG anarchist missed that memo.

There has never been a shortage of anarchists who get annoyed at other anarchists for ruining their club, but Bookchin’s caricature, the “lifestyle anarchist,” has bizarrely maintained a certain cachet among sectarians. This, despite the mismatched jumble of characteristics he cobbled together, and the documented revelation of his simultaneous rejection of anarchism – not just the “lifestyle” heresy. That he turned away from anarchism at the same time he slammed the tendencies that he found annoying should make even the most sectarian among us pause to consider the taint of Bookchin not actually wanting to “save” anarchism when his screed was published. Critical responses to SALA as well as other aspects of Murray Bookchin Thought include works by Bob Black , David Watson , Jason McQuinn , and others.

Meanwhile, two of the brightest stars in the ISE constellation, John Clark and Chuck Morse , came out of these destructive discussions with their eyes opened to much of what was wrong in Murray Bookchin Thought. Their post-mortems are well worth reading for anyone who might still believe that Bookchin was anything other than a bane on late-20 th century and early 21 st century anarchism.
