author: winter oak
title: The Erotic Life of a Mystic
content:
by Mark Josephs (aka Mark the Mystic Activist)

This is the most intimate article I’ve ever written. In it I describe my personal experience of awakening in an interconnected world in which everything is relating with everything.

Why do I define myself as a mystic? Because I look like one? Because I’m an old man living by myself, out in the countryside, off-grid, in a caravan? Because I wash outside, and meditate and pray? No.

I define myself as a mystic because my primary moment-to-moment interest is not in what’s happening, or even in what I’m doing – but in my relationship with The Totality (by whatever name).

When somebody prays, they feel they are in relationship with The Totality / God / Goddess / Great Mystery – obviously. But when somebody meditates deeply and “becomes one with everything”, there’s still the “with” word. That´s to say – there’s still a feeling of being in relationship.

I am interested in this relationship. I am interested in living in this relationship.

But first: the difficult question (and you might not like the answer!): is this relationship real? I might feel I am in relationship with The Totality, or my Idea of God or The Goddess – but does It feel Itself to be in relationship with me? Or (to be blunt): am I just imagining it?

I could give you clever answers about the infinite, interconnected complexity of existence, and the necessity of a coordinating intelligence – but any intellectual answer is only as reliable as the intellect. And the human intellect is clearly limited.

So let me be honest. I spend my days feeling I am in communion with The Totality. But am I really? I have no idea! Nor do I know how I could know!

I could make an appeal to the objectivity of intuition (“I just somehow know it to be true”), or to the objectivity of emotion (“I know it to be true because I can feel it”) – but, again, let’s be honest (otherwise what’s the point of discussing these matters: to just affirm each other’s preconceptions?): like the intellect, our intuitions and emotions are also subjective, conditioned and fallible.

But the exact same doubts about the reality of our perception apply to everything. How can we be certain of anything?! We perceive everything through limited, subjective, conditioned, fallible faculties! Does your lover love you? They say they do. You feel they do. But do they really? Can you prove it? No.

The truth of the matter, I believe, is that the only thing we can be certain of is uncertainty. Or, as Socrates reportedly declared: “I am the wisest of all, because I know I don’t know”.

We live in The Unknown. We don’t know where we are, or why. We don’t even perceive the world directly, but see its reflection on the screen of the mind – and therefore can’t even be certain of its reality. And so on.

So what to do? As Alan Watts said, “you´ve got to place your bet”. Your life is your betting chip, and you have to decide where to place it – whether on Universal Meaning or Universal Meaninglessness or Hedonism or Moralism or Guru Whoever or That Book… There are, of course, plenty of options.

So I have placed my bet, yes – on an ever-deepening relationship with The Totality. And as well as following Alan Watts’ advice, I also follow Joseph Campbell’s advice to “follow your bliss”. And he’s not talking about pleasure-seeking – he’s talking about something less easily defined: following that which makes our heart sing, following “the call of the soul” (John O’Donohue), following “the innermost decision that we cannot but obey” (Leonard Cohen).

I follow my bliss. And as I follow, the bliss increases! Does that prove the reality of Relationship with The Totality? (“You see – the relationship must be real, because the bliss just grows and grows!”) Not at all. It might just be that my hallucinatory state is expanding!

But what, for me, is this experience of relationship really like? I say it’s blissful. What else? What do I actually experience? What’s it like, for me, here in The Unknown, having placed my life-bet on the possibility of a real, reciprocatory relationship with The Totality?

The devotees of Krishna, the Sufis, and Christian mystics like Teresa of Avila and John of The Cross have all spoken of an erotic connection with The Totality. And I make this ‘appeal to authority’ (“you see, it’s not just me!”) because I am aware that people who speak about Sex with God (to be direct) can be easily misunderstood, and easily dismissed.

I don’t know exactly what those mystics experienced as they felt they were getting closer and closer to The Totality. But I imagine they felt more and more aroused – throughout their bodies (not just genitally). Because I do!

And I have guided many people along this path. And they all say – remarkably quickly and remarkably similarly – that as they breathe consciously, and bring their attention to their flesh – and let go of obstructive conditioning (like relationship with The Totality should be ‘pure, spiritual, disembodied’, or ‘distant, empty, neutral’, and so on – and definitely not ‘sexy’!) – and give themselves permission to really, really relax, and open, and become receptive ‘all the way down’ (from their heads, through their genitals, to their toes) – they too feel whole-body arousal – as if they were being penetrated by blessing.

I suppose that if my reference to famous mystics was a kind of ‘vertical appeal to authority’ – then letting you know how easily most of us can be guided into the Erotic Relationship with The Totality is a kind of ‘horizontal appeal to authority’- if you know what I mean. Once again “you see, it’s not just me!”

But I do have (what I consider to be) the good fortune to live on private land surrounded by Oaks – with Fig and Cherry Trees, and a dog, an allotment and chickens – where I can live naked outside – and where I don’t have to bow before The Clock God. Of course friends come and go, and I have a car, and drive off on errands, but generally it means that (in the way that I just explained I guide others) – I can guide myself full-time into The Arms of The Totality.

I say ‘The Arms of The Totality’ because I feel the presence of The Totality as an erotic embrace. Sometimes it’s more as if It is behind me, holding me from behind (a Mama Bear as Big as The Sky) – and sometimes it feels as if the embrace is all around me: right here, yet coming from everywhere – from as far away as I can imagine.

In this embrace I feel immovable, unshakeable, fearless. Yet also soft. My skin wakes up – as if responding to a tenderness in the air. Qualities we usually associate as ‘masculine’ arise in me: I feel powerful, absolutely still, silent, and solid – and at the same time I also feel what we would usually associate as a ‘feminine’ sexual longing – to be taken, to give myself, to surrender, to be enraptured.

I do feel living in nature helps. I can’t say “everyone should live in nature”, because everyone has their unique path – and who am I to say what others should or shouldn’t do?! But for me, there’s a huge difference between feeling myself in The Arms of God while surrounded by buildings, street lights and traffic – and feeling myself in The Arms of God in nature – where I feel myself to be ‘just another creature’ (like the trees, the birds, the insects) – all waking, sleeping, waking, sleeping – all breathing together – The Pulse of Life enlivening us all – the tender Kiss of Life passing through every body.

And (in contrast to the fashionably attired city centre) we’re all naked together! The trees are naked! The insects are naked! The chickens are naked! We’re not defended from That Which is Breathing Us All. We’re all surrendered to being-breathed. Something none of us understands is allowing us to all be alive – is keeping us all alive, moment-to-moment. It’s a wild Orgy of Life! (Again – I don’t know if it’s true or not, but) I am convinced the other creatures are all aroused too!

And then there’s ‘the L word’ – Love! Another delicate and easily misconstrued piece of language…

As I enter ever-deeper relationship with The Totality, my body opens – I live in the erotic pleasure of belonging. But my heart opens too. And that is very, very pleasurable too!

I recognise my Not Knowing – that (as we have discussed) I am perceiving my own, unique, limited, conditioned, subjective reality. I recognise I am a unique creature. And I recognise that everyone, of every species, is unique too.

And so I rest in my uniqueness, in The Totality’s Embrace – feeling I can make choices, but that, ultimately, I’m not in control of anything (even the functioning of my own body). And I feel happy to not be in control – happy to be held in the Erotic Embrace of The Infinite Mystery of Existence. From there, I meet other unique creatures…

Now (because I feel held in my uniqueness) I don’t compete with other people, or measure my worth by comparing myself with them, or require or resist their judgement – just as I don’t compete with the trees, or measure my worth comparing myself with the birds, or require or resist the judgement of the insects.

We are all unique. We are all held. Everyone is a wonder, in their own way.

I experience the embrace that holds each of us, and holds us all, as a Loving Embrace. In it – I feel loved. I feel I am loved as the unique creature I am. And because I am relaxed inside this love – when I meet others, I love them.

I see everyone as unique, and everyone as Held in the Loving Embrace of The Totality – whether that’s their conscious experience or not. In my eyes, they are loved – as I am loved. And as I am loved, I love them.

And there is a connection, I feel, in ways I don’t pretend to understand – between love and beauty. As I look out from The Erotic and Loving Holding of The Totality with eyes of love – everyone and everything looks brighter, more radiant, more beautiful.

And again, in ways I don’t pretend to understand – I feel that that beauty feeds me.

Like me, people I have guided also talk (as I said before: remarkably quickly and remarkably similarly) about no longer being in competition with others (once they’re rested in The Totality’s Embrace) – about feeling valued as unique beings, and therefore being able to value others as unique beings too – about feeling loved, and therefore being able to love. And about the beautification of the world.

My interest is in being in relationship with The Totality. That is very different from wanting to become ‘spiritually advanced’, or some such thing. I can be in relationship with The Totality – now, as I am.

I won’t ever be ‘more in relationship’ with The Totality than I am now. The relationship might deepen and mature (I hope it will) – but that will be an evolution of the quality of the relationship – not of our proximity.

How I can ever become ‘more part of The Totality’ than I am now?! My capacity to remain focused on feeling The Erotic Loving Embrace might develop. But I am convinced that The Totality will not love me more (when my attention-capacity is stronger), than it does now. I am convinced that It already loves me totally. Do we love adults more than we love adolescents, who we love more than we love children, who we love more than we love babies?! Of course not! Even we don’t love in proportion to people´s maturity.

That said – as we relax into The Erotic Embrace we observe ‘the monkey mind’ distracting us, and unintegrated shame, grief, fear and anger calling for our attention. But as we let ourselves Fall Into Love, and give generous space and kindness to everything that arises in our bodies, hearts and minds – gradually, gently, over time, our attention-capacity strengthens, and we find we are more and more uninterruptedly enjoying The Totality’s Embrace.

I feel this is important because many of us feel we need to make an effort to enter the Erotic and Loving Embrace of The Totality – when, in my opinion, all effort is counter-productive. In other words, as I see it: we already are Unique Expressions, or Unique Manifestations, of The Totality. We already belong. Continuous eroticism is already our birthright. We’re already loved. We don’t need to achieve anything. We just need to open to what’s already here – to soften, to let go, to relax, and open – and feel what we already are.

More about Mark’s philosophy of life can be found at https://www.tribusconscientes.com/

But I do have (what I consider to be) the good fortune to live on private land surrounded by Oaks – with Fig and Cherry Trees, and a dog, an allotment and chickens – where I can live naked outside – and where I don’t have to bow before The Clock God. Of course friends come and go, and I have a car, and drive off on errands, but generally it means that (in the way that I just explained I guide others) – I can guide myself full-time into The Arms of The Totality.

I say ‘The Arms of The Totality’ because I feel the presence of The Totality as an erotic embrace. Sometimes it’s more as if It is behind me, holding me from behind (a Mama Bear as Big as The Sky) – and sometimes it feels as if the embrace is all around me: right here, yet coming from everywhere – from as far away as I can imagine.

In this embrace I feel immovable, unshakeable, fearless. Yet also soft. My skin wakes up – as if responding to a tenderness in the air. Qualities we usually associate as ‘masculine’ arise in me: I feel powerful, absolutely still, silent, and solid – and at the same time I also feel what we would usually associate as a ‘feminine’ sexual longing – to be taken, to give myself, to surrender, to be enraptured.

I do feel living in nature helps. I can’t say “everyone should live in nature”, because everyone has their unique path – and who am I to say what others should or shouldn’t do?! But for me, there’s a huge difference between feeling myself in The Arms of God while surrounded by buildings, street lights and traffic – and feeling myself in The Arms of God in nature – where I feel myself to be ‘just another creature’ (like the trees, the birds, the insects) – all waking, sleeping, waking, sleeping – all breathing together – The Pulse of Life enlivening us all – the tender Kiss of Life passing through every body.

And (in contrast to the fashionably attired city centre) we’re all naked together! The trees are naked! The insects are naked! The chickens are naked! We’re not defended from That Which is Breathing Us All. We’re all surrendered to being-breathed. Something none of us understands is allowing us to all be alive – is keeping us all alive, moment-to-moment. It’s a wild Orgy of Life! (Again – I don’t know if it’s true or not, but) I am convinced the other creatures are all aroused too!
And then there’s ‘the L word’ – Love! Another delicate and easily misconstrued piece of language…
As I enter ever-deeper relationship with The Totality, my body opens – I live in the erotic pleasure of belonging. But my heart opens too. And that is very, very pleasurable too!

I recognise my Not Knowing – that (as we have discussed) I am perceiving my own, unique, limited, conditioned, subjective reality. I recognise I am a unique creature. And I recognise that everyone, of every species, is unique too.

And so I rest in my uniqueness, in The Totality’s Embrace – feeling I can make choices, but that, ultimately, I’m not in control of anything (even the functioning of my own body). And I feel happy to not be in control – happy to be held in the Erotic Embrace of The Infinite Mystery of Existence. From there, I meet other unique creatures…

Now (because I feel held in my uniqueness) I don’t compete with other people, or measure my worth by comparing myself with them, or require or resist their judgement – just as I don’t compete with the trees, or measure my worth comparing myself with the birds, or require or resist the judgement of the insects.
We are all unique. We are all held. Everyone is a wonder, in their own way.

I experience the embrace that holds each of us, and holds us all, as a Loving Embrace. In it – I feel loved. I feel I am loved as the unique creature I am. And because I am relaxed inside this love – when I meet others, I love them.

I see everyone as unique, and everyone as Held in the Loving Embrace of The Totality – whether that’s their conscious experience or not. In my eyes, they are loved – as I am loved. And as I am loved, I love them.

And there is a connection, I feel, in ways I don’t pretend to understand – between love and beauty. As I look out from The Erotic and Loving Holding of The Totality with eyes of love – everyone and everything looks brighter, more radiant, more beautiful.
And again, in ways I don’t pretend to understand – I feel that that beauty feeds me.

Like me, people I have guided also talk (as I said before: remarkably quickly and remarkably similarly) about no longer being in competition with others (once they’re rested in The Totality’s Embrace) – about feeling valued as unique beings, and therefore being able to value others as unique beings too – about feeling loved, and therefore being able to love. And about the beautification of the world.

My interest is in being in relationship with The Totality. That is very different from wanting to become ‘spiritually advanced’, or some such thing. I can be in relationship with The Totality – now, as I am.

I won’t ever be ‘more in relationship’ with The Totality than I am now. The relationship might deepen and mature (I hope it will) – but that will be an evolution of the quality of the relationship – not of our proximity.

How I can ever become ‘more part of The Totality’ than I am now?! My capacity to remain focused on feeling The Erotic Loving Embrace might develop. But I am convinced that The Totality will not love me more (when my attention-capacity is stronger), than it does now. I am convinced that It already loves me totally. Do we love adults more than we love adolescents, who we love more than we love children, who we love more than we love babies?! Of course not! Even we don’t love in proportion to people´s maturity.

That said – as we relax into The Erotic Embrace we observe ‘the monkey mind’ distracting us, and unintegrated shame, grief, fear and anger calling for our attention. But as we let ourselves Fall Into Love, and give generous space and kindness to everything that arises in our bodies, hearts and minds – gradually, gently, over time, our attention-capacity strengthens, and we find we are more and more uninterruptedly enjoying The Totality’s Embrace.

I feel this is important because many of us feel we need to make an effort to enter the Erotic and Loving Embrace of The Totality – when, in my opinion, all effort is counter-productive. In other words, as I see it: we already are Unique Expressions, or Unique Manifestations, of The Totality. We already belong. Continuous eroticism is already our birthright. We’re already loved. We don’t need to achieve anything. We just need to open to what’s already here – to soften, to let go, to relax, and open – and feel what we already are.
More about Mark’s philosophy of life can be found at https://www.tribusconscientes.com/

title: The Price of Gold: The Xingu River and the Communities Facing Destruction
content:
The Price of Gold: The Xingu River and the Communities Facing Destruction







Country







Brazil










agnes




Tue, 07/28/2026 - 10:50










Issues







Human Rights













Program







5













Main Image







 













By Angel Ferreira 

(Payayá, CS Intern)




At Volta Grande do Xingu, Brazil, two Indigenous communities, the Arara da Volta Grande and the Yudjá, continue to defend their ancestral territories against mounting external pressures. For the Yudjá, their name carries profound significance: it affirms their sovereignty and enduring relationship with the Xingu River, a bond that shapes their identity, culture, and way of life.




Today, however, their traditional livelihoods face a severe threat. The Volta Grande Project, backed by an estimated $229 million investment from Belo Sun Mineração Ltda., a subsidiary of Belo Sun Mining Corp., aims to establish one of the largest open-pit gold mines in the region. Community leaders and environmental experts warn that the project could inflict irreversible damage on a river system already deeply destabilized by the Belo Monte Hydroelectric Dam.




To understand the technical, social, and legal dimensions of this ongoing struggle, Cultural Survival spoke with anthropologist Thais Mantovanelli from the Instituto Socioambiental (ISA) / Xingu Program.










Thais Mantovanelli.


 




CS: With your experience of over a decade following the Juruna-Yudjá and Xikrin Peoples as well as the riverside communities, how are the mere expectations and pressure of Belo Sun's arrival already altering the social dynamics and mental health of these communities?




Thais Mantovanelli: 

The Volta Grande do Xingu region, composed of three Indigenous territories and hundreds of riverine families where Belo Sun intends to establish itself, currently faces the risk of reaching a point of no return, both environmentally and in terms of the social conditions required for the physical and cultural reproduction of these Peoples. This is because the chain of impacts from the operation system of the Belo Monte Hydroelectric Power Plant has weakened the region's ecological and social system far more aggressively than anticipated in the project's environmental impact studies. This terrifying scenario is well known to these collectives, whose current and ancestral traditional knowledge reinforces this catastrophic assessment.




Given this backdrop, the prospect of a mining project aiming to become the largest open-pit gold mine in the country severely impacts their social dynamics and mental health. It is an attack on the future of coming generations and on the maintenance of a cultural system intrinsically linked to the flood pulse of the Xingu River and its tributaries.




A climate of dread now governs the daily lives of these families, who are forced to mentally cope with the risk of human contamination associated with the mining project. The venture could cause shocks and instability in Belo Monte’s structures, such as the Pimental dam and other dikes, as well as the risk of a tailings dam failure, similar to what occurred in Brumadinho and Mariana. Other threats include the scaring off and poisoning of land animals on the islands; impacts on birds due to noise pollution from explosives (projected to operate 24/7 for at least 12 years); the death of fish species already scarce due to Belo Monte’s operating system; navigation risks; airborne pollutant dispersion; pressure on the territory caused by an influx of workers; and risks of sexual violence against girls and women in the territory due to the increase in unknown men arriving to join the mining project's workforce.




The threat of Belo Sun's installation represents a massive strain on the mental health of these collectives, who lose control over the management of their lives in both the present and the future.







CS: Volta Grande do Xingu is already experiencing ecocide caused by Belo Monte's "consensus hydrogram." From an anthropological and subsistence perspective, what would the overlay of a mega gold-mining project mean for these Peoples in this context of water scarcity?




TM:

 The current operating system of Belo Monte, through the consensus hydrogram, diverts 80% of the Xingu River's flood pulse during the flooding, high-water, and receding phases of the hydrological cycle, including the dry season. Indigenous and riverine Peoples of Volta Grande say that a river's flood pulse is like a person's heartbeat. They urge us to imagine what our own living conditions would be like if we could rely on only 20% of our heart rate, of our body's blood flow, which is vital to our existence. That is how the Xingu River is currently living: sickened and weakened, with only 20% of its flood pulse.




The fight for a fairer share of water for Volta Grande do Xingu is vital and urgent, as these collectives demonstrate. The MATI initiative (*Instituto de Pesquisa Intercultural e Monitoramento Independente da Volta Grande do Xingu* / Institute for Intercultural Research and Independent Monitoring of Volta Grande do Xingu) is one such movement fighting in this water dispute. Born from the intersection of traditional ecosystemic knowledge from local Peoples and academic knowledge from natural and social sciences, MATI produces ecological and social data on Belo Monte's impacts and fights to be included in the hydroelectric project's environmental licensing process.




Since 2023, IBAMA (Brazilian Institute of Environment and Renewable Natural Resources) has recognized the scientific validity of the initiative's analyses and agrees on the need for a fairer water allocation based on multiple uses, rather than being calculated exclusively for electricity generation. The dispute over water in Volta Grande do Xingu must also account for the climate emergency, increasing deforestation rates in the Xingu socioecological corridor, and decreasing rainfall in the region, which leads to extreme droughts and worsening living conditions for animals, plants, and people. The water volumes defended by the concessionaire Norte Energia for Belo Monte's operating system via the consensus hydrogram ignore the reality of the climate emergency and exacerbate it through the imposition of this water stress.




The installation of Belo Sun's mining project in a territory already experiencing a water dispute is ecologically, socially, and culturally unviable. The Canadian mining company's project ignores this context and fails to present cumulative impact studies considering Belo Monte's operation, an essential requirement for analyzing any new project or venture in Volta Grande do Xingu.







CS: The right to Free, Prior and Informed Consent and ILO Convention 169 is frequently undermined in these processes. How do you evaluate the quality and legitimacy of the dialogue that Belo Sun and the State have attempted to establish with local leaders?




TM: 

First, we must emphasize that for a consultation process to be free and informed, it must be *prior*, meaning it must address an initial idea or proposal, never a fully finalized project. This means that to comply with ILO Convention 169 requirements, the consultation must occur during the project's feasibility study phase, not during environmental licensing. The consultation process regarding the Belo Sun project violated this temporal principle because it was conducted after the issuance of the Prior License (*Licença Prévia*), which was later suspended so that consultations could take place.




The informative nature mandated by ILO Convention 169 was also neglected by Belo Sun. The scope of consultations conducted so far by the Canadian company and its third-party contractors was not properly informative. Critical details are missing regarding the project's operational mechanics, the extent of impacts associated with planned activities, and mitigation actions for each set of impacts. From a regulatory perspective under Convention 169, it is impossible to validate a consultation for a mining project that lacks complete details on the structure and operation of the tailings dam meant for storing toxic waste. Belo Sun failed to provide this information even after SEMAS (Secretariat of Environment and Sustainability of Pará) demanded a revision of the structural proposal.




Similarly, it is crucial that a mine closure plan be outlined and presented for consultation, which did not happen in Belo Sun's case. The Canadian company's mining exploitation project lacks any plan for closing the tailings dam following the proposed gold extraction period in Volta Grande.







CS: Large mining projects often use tactics that fragment the social fabric of communities, generating internal divisions. How have the Peoples of Volta Grande organized and resisted these co-optation attempts or individual negotiations?




TM: 

This is a crucial question, and we must highlight how violent and unfair these co-optation processes are, especially considering the emotional, social, and economic vulnerability of the Indigenous Peoples and riverine communities of Volta Grande do Xingu, who depended on fishing for food security and financial independence. These collectives have faced abrupt disruptions to their way of life since the licensing, construction, and operation of Belo Monte. The imposition of reduced water flow forced them to adapt to "living on dry land," seeking economic alternatives in agricultural activities outside their cultural tradition, such as cocoa planting. These activities are almost always ineffective as a replacement for the income previously earned through fishing.




Thus, we must stress the complexity at play in Belo Sun's licensing and the violations linked to co-optation efforts directed by the Canadian miner and its contractors at these vulnerable populations. Another dimension of violence caused by Belo Sun's licensing process is the creation of a hostile environment among relatives and neighbors in Volta Grande, leading to socio-affective ruptures that are difficult to heal. We see that the entire burden of Belo Sun is placed onto the impacted Indigenous and riverine communities, who should be protected under Brazilian constitutional and environmental law.




Despite this context of burden-shifting, local and regional collective responses have emerged as uprisings against the mining venture and its violations. The most prominent of these uprisings is led by women from various Indigenous ethnicities and riverine communities in the Middle Xingu region, demanding the suspension of Belo Sun's environmental licensing. Altamira, Belém, and Brasília have served as stages for these demonstrations, witnessing an explicit refusal sung by Middle Xingu women through the Mẽbengokre phrase *Belo Sun Akató* ("Out with Belo Sun").




CS: Riverine communities often face greater legal invisibility than Indigenous Peoples in licensing processes. How does the threat of Belo Sun specifically affect the territorial recognition and lifestyle of these non-Indigenous riverine residents?




TM

: The social composition of Volta Grande is as diverse as its ecological structure. This multicultural and biodiverse character, which should be protected, is one of the aspects most damaged during environmental licensing processes, whether for infrastructure works or mining projects.




It is worth highlighting that the territorial situation of riverine communities in Volta Grande do Xingu significantly increases their vulnerability. Many families and communities lack legal land titles for their traditional territories and live with the daily insecurity of land conflicts. Even families living in land reform settlements recognized by INCRA (National Institute for Colonization and Agrarian Reform) report cases of violence and threats characteristic of regional land disputes, which have intensified with the prospect of Belo Sun’s installation. Several families abandoned their lands following threats due to their public opposition to the Canadian mining project.




Although the State Public Defender's Office and the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office have filed public civil actions to protect these communities, insecurity remains a daily reality. Many of these collectives, also impacted by Belo Monte, have not received proper mitigation and suffer various rights violations, including lack of access to drinking water, loss of river navigation, lack of roads, communication isolation, loss of food security and income, and the inefficacy of productive activity programs under Belo Monte's Basic Environmental Plan (PBA).




Having been excluded from consultations during Belo Monte’s licensing, these collectives continue to see their right to consultation violated by Belo Sun. Rendered invisible, riverine families were not even granted access to the environmental impact studies for the Canadian mining project. They remain unaware of the project's structure as well as the technical reports criticizing the proposal due to pollution risks and the lack of cumulative impact analyses, which are essential in a Volta Grande already altered by Belo Monte.







CS: Given the history of Belo Monte, what is the main lesson that the Peoples of Volta Grande do Xingu use today to try to prevent this history of rights violations from repeating itself with Belo Sun?




TM

: The resilience of the Indigenous Peoples and riverine communities of Volta Grande do Xingu is truly incredible as they continue fighting to free the river's waters and preserve the migratory fish runs (*piracemas*). The MATI initiative and the mobilization of Middle Xingu women demonstrate the strength and boldness of those fighting for their right to exist.




Nevertheless, as a democratic society based on the rule of law, we must recognize that protecting these traditional collectives in Volta Grande do Xingu against socioenvironmental violations must be genuinely assumed as a matter of State policy, not left solely to the actions of communities already deeply weakened by Belo Monte.




The licensing process of Belo Monte teaches a bitter lesson: in Brazil, the pursuit of profit in development projects like hydroelectric power plants and large-scale mining has been prioritized over the defense of traditional Peoples, their territories, and their cultural rights. The very collectives that protect forests and waters are the ones left bearing the environmental and cultural losses of these polluting projects. As a society, we urgently need to rebalance this equation.







To learn more about the ongoing resistance and technical counter-assessments, visit the official platform of the Aliança Volta Grande do Xingu (

voltagrandexingu.org

). The Alliance brings together Indigenous Peoples, riverine communities, socio-environmental organizations, and researchers dedicated to defending the Xingu River basin against destructive megaprojects.




Their portal serves as a critical repository for independent scientific monitoring, human rights reports, and community-led declarations detailing the cumulative impacts of Belo Monte and the Belo Sun mining proposal.




You can also support the movement directly by signing the international petition against the Canadian mining company:

 Petition Against Belo Sun

. The petition demands the immediate revocation of Belo Sun's installation license and urges Brazilian federal authorities to respect the constitutional rights and sovereignty of traditional territories.

title: Del vino al cobre: el cambio estructural que sufrió Mendoza durante el boom del cobre
content:
Desarrollo del Distrito Minero Malargüe (

Gobierno de Mendoza/2024

)




Durante dos décadas, Mendoza fue emblema de la resistencia a la megaminería. Sin embargo, la crisis de sectores tradicionales como el sector vitivinícola y turístico, el avance de la transición energética y una estrategia política que ha buscado aumentar la explotación han cambiado el panorama. Hoy la provincia impulsa 65 proyectos exploratorios de cobre que hace solo tres años no estaban aprobados y debate cómo compatibilizar la minería con la defensa histórica del agua. 

P

or Andrés Mauricio Díaz Páez y Matías Avramow, para Climate Tracker América Latina.







En la apertura de sesiones legislativas de 2025, el gobernador de Mendoza, en Argentina, Alfredo Cornejo, presentó frente a todos los representantes de la provincia dos objetos con una carga simbólica tremenda: una botella de vino y una roca aturquesada repleta de cobre. “Este producto [levantando la roca con sus manos] puede darle riqueza a Mendoza, contribuir al ambiente del mundo en la electromovilidad y tiene una demanda internacional clave para las próximas décadas; no tiene por qué ser incompatible con el vino”, declaró en un acto que consolidó una transformación estructural que llevaba años desarrollándose.




Fue claro, a partir de ahí, que el gobierno provincial empujaría con fuerza un cambio productivo resistido durante décadas, ya que entre 2003 y 2019 Mendoza fue considerada “antiminera”, no solo por la población civil sino también por cámaras empresariales como la vitivinícola y la turística. Hace solo siete años no existía ningún proyecto minero activo aprobado en la provincia y no fue hasta 2023 que apareció la exploración cuprífera; hoy hay 65 en exploración y uno en construcción. Salvo contadas excepciones —un proyecto de litio, uno de hierro y otro de potasio—, la prioridad es el cobre. 







En una revisión del 

mapa oficial de catastro minero

 de la provincia, esta alianza periodística identificó 64 zonificaciones —que incluyen distintas etapas del proceso administrativo en minería como proyectos de exploración, cateos, manifestaciones y minas— que se superponen a sitios inventariados como áreas glaciales por el gobierno nacional o naturales protegidas por la ley provincial, que prohíbe la minería en polígonos de ese tipo. 




Jimena Latorre, ministra de Energía y Ambiente de Mendoza, aclaró que todas estas son categorías administrativas dentro del proceso minero y que en Mendoza, salvo por el Proyecto San Jorge (PSJ), “todo es exploratorio”, por lo cual “no se está comprometiendo el agua” provincial. “En muchos casos son incluso tareas de escritorio”, sumó, y declaró: “Cualquier empresa que empieza actividades exploratorias lo hace con la visión de poder tener descubrimientos y pasar a producción. Pero los indicadores muestran que solo uno de cada cien proyectos que se exploran pasa a esa etapa. Ni en exploración ni en producción se autorizará nada que no cumpla con la normativa”.




Este esquema productivo ha generado resistencia de varios miembros de la sociedad civil, en particular debido al riesgo que para ellos significa la disputa por el agua y el incumplimiento de regulaciones ambientales. 




Esta provincia se localiza cerca de la cordillera de los Andes, justo al otro lado de Santiago de Chile, y en una de las zonas más áridas de Argentina. En promedio, las precipitaciones rondan los 200 milímetros al año, una cifra parecida a la que se registra en la península colombiana de La Guajira o en el Valle de Tehuacán, en México.




Allí, donde hay verde es porque pasa alguno de los pocos ríos o sistemas de riego que, en su totalidad, se abastecen del deshielo glaciar o de la nieve que cae en la alta montaña durante una sola temporada al año. Una que, de acuerdo con estudios recientes, decayó con fuerza en la 

última década debido a lo que llaman una “megasequía

”.




Relación entre la media de caudales y el máximo de acumulación anual de nieve en los Andes centrales, donde se encuentra Mendoza (Mariano Masiokas-Ianigla/2026)




Desde su fundación, esta provincia tuvo al agua como parte sensible y vital de su organización política y social. Una de las primeras leyes que se promulgaron, en 1884, 

fue la Ley de Aguas

, que, en términos generales, prioriza este recurso para el consumo humano, después para la agricultura y, por último, para la industria. Ese mismo año también se creó el Departamento General de Irrigación, que administra con autonomía las contadas concesiones de agua.




“En realidad, el agua apta para consumo es un recurso escaso. Ahí podríamos discutir sobre infraestructura e inversiones para llevar esa agua a los centros de consumo. Pero más allá de eso, el agua, como recurso natural, es determinante en todas las provincias cordilleranas”, explicó Latorre.




El cobre jamás había ocupado un lugar tan central en la economía mundial como ahora. Su importancia se multiplicó con el desarrollo de los primeros sistemas eléctricos comerciales a principios del siglo pasado, pero lo que hoy vemos parece superar cualquier etapa anterior. De acuerdo con un 

reporte de 2026 de la Agencia Internacional de Energía (IEA), por sus siglas en inglés)

, la demanda por el mineral sigue en aumento, pasando de 24.946 kt en 2021, a más de 31 mil kt esperadas para 2030. 




La transición energética, 

advierte

 la Conferencia de las Naciones Unidas sobre Comercio y Desarrollo (Unctad, por sus siglas en inglés), es “fundamentalmente intensiva en minerales”. Paneles solares, turbinas eólicas, vehículos eléctricos y redes para transportar la electricidad dependen de una larga lista de esos elementos que hoy son considerados estratégicos y cuya demanda, 

según proyecciones

 de la IEA, podría duplicarse en las próximas décadas.




Con un detalle no menor: China demanda casi el 60% del cobre del mundo, de acuerdo con datos de la misma agencia, con un promedio de 26,96 millones de toneladas de acuerdo a 

registros de UNComtrade

. Sin embargo, el panorama actual de los proyectos de extracción de cobre —con limitados descubrimientos de yacimientos, aumento de costos y largos plazos de ejecución— apunta a una posible falta del 30% de suministro global para 2035.




A 35 kilómetros de Uspallata, en la base del cerro San Jorge está en construcción el Proyecto San Jorge, el primero que extraerá cobre mendocino (LPA/2025)




La provincia “antiminera”




Federico Soria es uno de los más antiguos referentes sociales de la localidad de Uspallata que se encuentra a cuatro horas de la ciudad de Mendoza y cuyos habitantes se han movilizado desde 1993 para evitar el desarrollo de la minería en la provincia. Desde 2008 forma parte de la Asamblea de Vecinos de Uspallata por el Agua, que buscaba específicamente frenar el avance del Proyecto San Jorge, una mina de cobre que estuvo 

prohibida hasta diciembre de 2025, cuando su Declaración de Impacto Ambiental

 [requisito indispensable para avanzar] fue aprobada por ambas cámaras legislativas en una sesión exprés. Fue un momento que, fuera del recinto, en la calle, se vivió con una violencia que Soria describió como inédita.




Los manifestantes fueron

 amedrentados con bastonazos y gas lacrimógeno

. “Hubo 41 manifestantes detenidos. Les armaron procesos penales a muchos. Un grupo de abogados viene defendiendo a los imputados en esas causas y hace poco interpusieron una demanda ante la Comisión Interamericana de Derechos Humanos contra el gobierno de Mendoza”, agregó el activista. 




Ninguna de las fuentes consultadas niega que la situación es muy distinta a conflictos anteriores con el PSJ o con la minería en general. No es solo por el “intento disciplinador del gobierno para callar las voces que están en contra de la minería”, como lo mencionó un asesor legislativo de la oposición mendocina que pidió no revelar su nombre. Hay un reconocimiento de que el consenso en contra de la megaminería que existía en 2003 y que se mantuvo sólido al menos hasta 2017 menguó. Esto, de acuerdo con varios analistas consultados, se debió a factores políticos y estructurales.




En 2007 había movimientos sociales acompañados por dos de los sectores productivos más fuertes de la provincia, opuestos al desarrollo minero: la industria del turismo y, por supuesto, la del vino. También había una Legislatura heterogénea que, de acuerdo con lo que describió Marcelo Giraud, geógrafo y dirigente social provincial, veía en la oposición a la megaminería una parte de su estandarte político.




Movilizaciones en Uspallata en contra del Proyecto San Jorge (Asamblea de Vecinos Autoconvocados de Uspallata/2025)




En aquel año se sancionó la 

Ley de Medio Ambiente, Sustancias Tóxicas, Exploración y Explotación de Minerales

, conocida popularmente como la 7722. En su artículo 1°, este documento estipula que está prohibido el uso de “sustancias químicas como cianuro, mercurio, ácido sulfúrico y otras sustancias tóxicas similares en los procesos mineros metalíferos de cateo, prospección, exploración, explotación y/o industrialización de minerales metalíferos obtenidos a través de cualquier método extractivo”. En conjunto con la Ley de Aguas y la de Protección de Flora y Fauna, conforman la regulación provincial más fuerte sobre minería y uso del agua.




Un año después de que se sancionara la 7722, se anunció el inicio del PSJ y la reacción social fue casi automática. Para 2009 ya había movilizaciones masivas no solo en Uspallata, sino también en otras ciudades de la provincia. Para 2011, la mayoría de la Legislatura mendocina votó en contra de la aprobación del proyecto en un recinto rodeado por la sociedad civil.




Muchos legisladores que hoy son funcionarios del actual gobernador Alfredo Cornejo se sumaron a esa consigna. “En aquella época, muchos políticos no se atrevían a hablar de minería en su campaña por temor a perder votos”, recordó Itatí Brida, activista de Uspallata que desde 2008 milita en la Asamblea de Vecinos por el Agua.




Varios representantes mineros pidieron la inconstitucionalidad de la 7722, pero en 2015 fue ratificada por la 

Suprema Corte de Mendoza

 y en 2021 por la 

Corte Suprema de Justicia de la Nación

 —con cuestionamientos sobre indefiniciones puntuales—. En 2017, bajo el gobierno de Cornejo, también se intentó derogar aquella ley, aunque diez días después revirtieron la medida debido a numerosas manifestaciones. “Los cortes de ruta fueron en todos lados. Recuerdo que acá sosteníamos el corte entre muchos vecinos. Fueron de toda la provincia a la capital para presionar. Fue masivo”, sumó Brida. Para ese entonces, en otras partes de la provincia, como Malargüe, ya habían avanzado varios proyectos de exploración minera en proceso de consolidación. 




La sociedad civil mendocina ha estado muy activa a la hora de aceptar el desarrollo minero en la provincia (Asamblea de Vecinos Autoconvocados de Uspallata/2025)




Cambios en la estructura




La industria con mayor potencia en Mendoza, la del vino, ha caído con mucha fuerza desde 2017. Un 

estudio elaborado por el Instituto de Estudios sobre la Realidad Argentina y Latinoamericana (Ieral), en conjunto con la Fundación Mediterránea

 y publicado en 2025, registró esta contracción sostenida y planteó que ese año fue el más bajo en poco más de 15 años.




“Hoy la minería tiene una licencia social de la que no gozaba hace unos años. Con la retracción del poder adquisitivo, las personas ven que una posibilidad como la minería puede ser un aliciente para un grupo de personas y generar puestos de trabajo”, describió Fabián Ruggeri, presidente de la Corporación Vitivinícola Argentina (Coviar), la federación de cámaras de esta industria, institutos técnicos y los gobiernos de Mendoza y San Juan. “No podemos desechar la realidad de que esto, nos opongamos o no nos opongamos, va a pasar. Es más práctico y más lógico acompañar ese proceso, pero, por supuesto, con todos los controles que correspondan”, advirtió.




Ruggeri aseguró también que gran parte de los valles productivos de Mendoza se encuentra en cuencas que en este momento no comparten agua con las minas. La zona de Malargüe, que es la que más proyectos mineros concentra, está al suroeste de la provincia, donde no hay producción agrícola alguna. Los ríos que pasan cerca de esa zona son endorreicos —es decir, no tienen salida al mar— o atraviesan otras provincias, como es el caso del río Atuel, que sigue por La Pampa y llega hasta la provincia de Buenos Aires.




Como lo describió Brida, las empresas más grandes que concentran el consumo del agua —las del vino y la agricultura— “son parte de la gente que cambió de postura. Entraron a poner sus activos en la minería. Las pequeñas pymes y los pequeños productores están con nosotros”, señaló. Ruggeri no dio precisiones sobre estos grandes grupos, pero coincidió en que, sobre todo los más grandes, son grupos corporativos multirubro y también tienen inversiones mineras, algo que no ve como un problema.




“La base es que el resto de la superficie de la provincia presenta potencialidad para energía y minería que son perfectamente compatibles con la agricultura. ¿Por qué? Porque hay un marco normativo que lo garantiza”, planteó, en la misma línea, la ministra de Energía y Ambiente mendocina, Jimena Latorre.




Pozas en la reigón de Malargüe, en la provincia de Mendoza (Cámara de Turismo de Mendoza)




Los movimientos sociales descreen de esa declaración. En Uspallata, con el caso del PSJ, los vecinos movilizados piensan que el avance minero podría flexibilizar las normativas. Tanto es así que desde la aprobación de la DIA de ese proyecto minero ya presentaron tres recursos de amparo para detenerla.




“Dos fueron rechazados por la Justicia, pero uno sigue en pie”, resaltó Brida. También sometieron ante la Legislatura la creación de un Área Natural Protegida en la zona donde la minera está construyendo sus instalaciones. “De esa manera sería ilegal la actividad”, comentó Soria. Desde hace casi diez años esta propuesta descansa en el recinto sin perder estado parlamentario, pero tampoco consigue los votos suficientes para ser aprobada.




Esta alianza les preguntó cuál sería la alternativa a la minería, en un contexto de transición energética, a los sectores movilizados. Soria respondió lo siguiente: “La postura es que lo valioso del territorio es su agua, su gente y que es elegido por esto. El turismo y los visitantes disfrutan de la naturaleza como nosotros. Creo que esa es la postura que tenemos. Creo que la transición energética, tal como la vemos, requiere del sacrificio de lugares como el nuestro. A nosotros nos hablan de la transición energética, pero no sabemos eso. No sabemos si lo van a usar para la industria bélica o para la industria aeronáutica. Y además, ¿cuál transición energética? ¿La que impulsan los mismos emisores de gases de efecto invernadero?”.

content:
7 Actions to Take on Int'l Day of the World's Indigenous Peoples 2026

August 9 is

 International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples

 (August 9). Every day, we honor the sovereignty, richness, and beauty of Indigenous Peoples, languages, and lifeways.




The first meeting of the

 United Nations Working Group on Indigenous Populations

 was held in Geneva, Switzerland, on August 9, 1982. Since then, many spaces have opened up for Indigenous voices to be heard, and new agreements protecting the rights of Indigenous Peoples have been adopted. While we celebrate these outcomes, we also recognize that the promise of human rights for Indigenous Peoples worldwide remains unfulfilled. In many parts of the world, Indigenous Peoples are still facing grave human rights abuses and challenges.





This year's theme is 

“Honouring Indigenous Midwives: Safeguarding Life and Well-being.”




Indigenous Peoples, our values, and knowledge systems hold solutions to today’s greatest challenges, including climate change, ecocide, and biodiversity loss. But all too often, we are not listened to, consulted, nor given seats at the tables where important decisions that impact us are being made. At Cultural Survival, we are working around the world and around the clock to support the priorities of Indigenous Nations and communities that are protecting Mother Earth for generations to come and for the millions of people, plant, animal, and mineral relatives that share our homelands.




 










 




7 Actions to Take on Int'l Day of the World's Indigenous Peoples










1. Demand Justice for Indigenous Defenders in Mexico and Colombia







Join the 

In Memoriam Campaign for Justice for Indigenous Defenders

 killed in Mexico and Colombia, where Indigenous defenders continue to face deadly violence for defending their rights, lands, and territories.

Read our latest issue of the 

Cultural Survival Quarterly

 magazine. "Pathways to Healing: Indigenous Sovereignty, Traditional Knowledge and Collective Well Being"





Celebrating 50 years of publishing and amplifying Indigenous voices! This issue highlights holistic systems of care rooted in ancestral wisdom informing the present and shaping the future of our communities. title: El gobierno de Neuquén insiste en desconocer a comunidades Mapuches
content:
Las comunidades originarias de la provincia de Neuquén vienen sufriendo distintos tipos de violencia y amenazas, que además están muy perjudicada por el tremendo avance extractivista con complicidad estatal.

https://argentina.indymedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Kay-Pacha-Cardenas.mp3

Entre el peligro de la contaminación a causa del sistema de fracking que utilizan los extractivismos, y que no sólo alcanza a los territorios, sino también a las aguas de los espacios hídricos en la zona, también se encuentra el negacionismo a reconocer las comunidades mapuches.

Uno de los ejemplos más conocidos es el caso de las comunidades Rañileo Cárdenas y Kelv Kura, quienes vienen solicitando sus personerías jurídicas desde hace varios años y siempre les piden más y más requisitos. Sobre estas personerías, que son su documento de identidad como comunidades mapuche, luego de que el propio Ministro Jorge Tobares les afirmara que el 99% de las mismas estaba aprobada, por un año no encontraron respuesta.

Por eso los hermanos y hermanas decidieron hacer permanencia frente a la casa de gobierno, de donde luego de 5 días fueron desalojados violentamente.  De este hecho, el pasado 20 de julio, se  cumplió hace exactamente un año, donde hubo más de 18 detenidos, hombres, mujeres y niños golpeados.

Y ahora es entonces cuando el Ministro Tobares a través de la Res. 155/26 completa su política de negación de derechos DENEGANDO las Personerías a estas dos comunidades.

Cabe destacar que, por un lado, cuando estaban en la permanencia, el Obispo de Neuquén había comprometido una mediación para el día después y el Ministro de Gobierno había aceptado esa gestión.

Sorpresivamente, el día antes, un día domingo las familias se vieron rodeadas de policías antimotines, carros hidrantes y motos, que repentinamente hicieron sentir toda su violencia para escarmentar su reclamo de derechos.

También existió una mediación con la Universidad Nacional del Comahue, cuyos técnicos visitaron la zona y elaboraron un informe que acredita sus derechos a esos territorios.

Entonces ahora vamos a escuchar el testimonio del lonko Nelson Ragileo Cárdenas, quien explica varias situaciones que vienen soportando en su  lucha por este reconocimiento.

El Micro Kay Pacha se realiza con el apoyo de la organización Otto per Mille-Chiessa Valdense.

La entrada El gobierno de Neuquén insiste en desconocer a comunidades Mapuches se publicó primero en Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i )) .

author: Darío Aranda
title: Marchar por la tierra sin olvidar los despojos del pasado y del presente
content:
Por Adrián Moyano*

Sí, claro. ¿Cómo no vamos a marchar el jueves 6 de agosto por las tierras? Pero déjenme pasar un par de avisos: la primera extranjerización significativa de la historia que nos incumbe la llevó a cabo el Estado argentino a través de su brazo armado. Los corrimientos de la línea de fortines fueron paulatinos desde la década de 1820 en adelante, pero el ritmo de la usurpación se tornó vertiginoso y mortal a partir de 1878.

Me permito recordar que para 1810 la frontera entre el antiguo Virreinato del Río de la Plata y el territorio de los pueblos indígenas libres, entre ellos el mapuche, pasaba a dos o tres galopitos de Buenos Aires. Y fue junto con los rémingtons y los sables que llegó la propiedad privada.

El monumental despojo no benefició inicialmente en nada al pueblo argentino. Es más, en la época de "la manteca al techo" la clase trabajadora sufría condiciones de explotación espantosas, las que también comenzaron a padecer culturas que no eran perfectas, pero nunca habían puesto en el centro de su funcionamiento la plusvalía.

Cuando buena parte de los y las mapuche sobrevivientes todavía languidecía en campos de concentración, su antiguo territorio se fraccionó y quedó en manos de militares de alto nivel que se llenaban la boca con invocaciones a la patria, entre ellos, el propio Roca. Por dar un par de ejemplos, un año después de que muriera Inakayal, la Compañía de Tierras del Sud Argentino ya poseía una cantidad de hectáreas que incluso vulneraba la legislación vigente y en parte de los antiguos dominios del lonco Reuque Cura se instaló la Estancia Pulmarí, también de capitales británicos. De ese origen fue el Ferrocarril del Sud, que unió Bahía Blanca con el Alto Valle del río Negro y después con Zapala. ¿Se imaginan a cuánto trepó la cotización de las tierras que hasta 1879 recorrieron en libertad las caravanas mapuches y tehuelches?

Claro que vamos a marchar el jueves, pero desde que se reformó la Constitución Nacional (1994), ningún gobierno reconoció --como dicta la ley suprema del país-- “la posesión y propiedad comunitarias de las tierras que tradicionalmente ocupan” las comunidades indígenas y menos aún se dignó “regular la entrega de otras aptas y suficientes para el desarrollo humano”. Pasaron 32 años y no sé cuántas gestiones. Como la “tierra indígena” no es “enajenable, transmisible ni susceptible de gravámenes o embargos”, los títulos de propiedad comunitaria serían barricadas infranqueables ante la profundización del despojo que ahora requiere el funcionamiento capitalista.

Por último, déjenme sumar que la Ley 26.160 que ordenó el Relevamiento Territorial de Comunidades Indígenas estuvo en vigencia durante 18 años y no se terminó en ningún lado. ¿Inoperancia o decisión política? ¿Cómo puede ser que, superado el primer cuarto del siglo XXI, el Estado en sus diversas jurisdicciones no sepa cuáles son los territorios indígenas? Si hasta tiene herramientas para saber si ampliamos el galponcito del fondo.

Vamos a marchar, claro que sí. Pero después no me vengan con que “hay que aprovechar las ventajas que nos da el mercado internacional”. Con esa excusa llenaron de soja hasta los maceteros. O con que “hay que pensar a la cordillera como una torta”.

* Periodista y escritor . Autor de numerosos libros, entre ellos "Crónicas de la resistencia mapuche" y "A ruego de mi superior cacique, Inakayal".

La entrada Marchar por la tierra sin olvidar los despojos del pasado y del presente se publicó primero en Agencia de Noticias Tierra Viva .

author: Elyse Wild
title: As Screens Take Over, Advocates Say Play, Culture Are Key to Native Youth Mental Health
content:
The answer to a growing mental health crisis in a world in which screens are omnipresent and social media is fueling a sense of despair among the nation’s young people may be simple: get outside and play.

That’s according to a new report by Kaboom!, a nonprofit that builds playgrounds around the nation. The report was created in collaboration with IndigiFit Kids , a three-year campaign by the Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux Community aimed at improving the physical and mental health of Native youth in Minnesota.

The report outlines data that shows mental health among the nation’s young people is plummeting, and Native youth are the most at risk. Increased screen time, reduced physical activity, slashed recess times, and more than 28 million kids lacking access to a green space or playground point to a shrinking childhood. From 2017 to 2021, depression diagnoses among children rose by 60%, with anxiety rising by 31%. While the issue touches every community, Native communities bear the brunt: suicide rates among Native youth ages 15 to 19 are double that of white youth. But among the bleak numbers, there is hope: kids who spend 60 minutes a day in nature have a 50% lower risk of mental health issues.

Disconnection

Dr. Mark Baez (Coahuiltecan Tribe) is the president of the Society for Indian Psychologists, whose clinic work focuses on adolescents and children. Baez told Native News Online that the issues driving the plummeting youth mental health are compounded in Native communities by the lasting effects of colonialism: poverty, generational trauma, geographic isolation, and loss of culture through federal campaigns to erase Native Americans.

“Many youth carry both online and historical trauma stressors simultaneously,” Baez said.

Those stressors, he said, result in a sense of isolation, antithetical to the core of many Native cultures and communities: connection.

“As clinicians, some of the signs that we see are loneliness, depression, anxiety, difficulty maintaining face-to-face relationships,” Baez said. “For Native youth, we see a lot of our kids on social media being digitally connected while simultaneously feeling disconnected from their family, community, culture, and peers.”

While putting down the phones and getting outside to play might be part of the solution, Native communities are seriously lacking in accessible, safe play spaces compared to other communities. An assessment of 237 playgrounds on or near tribal lands and urban areas with high Native populations found nearly 70% posed safety hazards, with varying degrees of repair and replacement needed.

Ashley Cornforth, Secretary-Treasurer for the Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux, told Native News Online building play spaces for youth can be part of a tribe’s stewardship of their land and seven-generations planning.

“We have a connection to our ancestral land,” she said. “We’re always going to be here. Play spaces are so integral to getting out and playing, and that physical activity has such a connection to mental health. How do we show that we want to maintain it? We want to make it stay good for our next youth.”

Screen Time

While the effects have been clear for many years, a 2021 Wall Street Journal investigation confirmed what many parents suspected: social media harms children’s mental health, and the tech giants behind the most popular apps are well aware. In recent years, Tribal Nations have filed suit against the social media companies , including Meta, Snap, ByteDance, and Alphabet, for their role in the youth mental health and suicide crisis plaguing Native communities. The suits point to addictive algorithms, gambling-like features, and exploitation of reciprocity.

On top of being designed to draw youth in over and over again, social media can provide ample opportunity for cruel bullying, far from the eyes of adults.

“We think, ‘just walk away, close the screen,’ right?” Baez said. “It’s easier said than done. The exposure to trauma and harmful content is very real: bullying, racism, lateral violence, misinformation. It has real harm.”

While the prevalence of screens in modern life may make screen time feel like an insurmountable obstacle for parents, both Baez and Cornforth said that healing Native youth and bringing them back to their culture starts with adults.

“If we want them to put their phones away, we need to do the same,” Baez said. “It sounds cliché, but kids are sponges, so lead by example. We need to create opportunities for youth to engage. Culture is prevention, and I go a step further: culture is medicine, because this culture is what has given us the ability to be resilient.”

Listen

Technology has become such a connector. I can talk to my cousins now, or I can talk to my grandma. And before, I didn’t have that. I didn’t have that connection to culture or language.”

That talking circle represents what Cornforth said needs to be at the center of helping Native kids thrive: listening to them.

contentBlocks.text: The answer to a growing mental health crisis in a world in which screens are omnipresent and social media is fueling a sense of despair among the nation’s young people may be simple: get outside and play.

That’s according to a new report by Kaboom!, a nonprofit that builds playgrounds around the nation. The report was created in collaboration with IndigiFit Kids , a three-year campaign by the Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux Community aimed at improving the physical and mental health of Native youth in Minnesota.

The report outlines data that shows mental health among the nation’s young people is plummeting, and Native youth are the most at risk. Increased screen time, reduced physical activity, slashed recess times, and more than 28 million kids lacking access to a green space or playground point to a shrinking childhood. From 2017 to 2021, depression diagnoses among children rose by 60%, with anxiety rising by 31%. While the issue touches every community, Native communities bear the brunt: suicide rates among Native youth ages 15 to 19 are double that of white youth. But among the bleak numbers, there is hope: kids who spend 60 minutes a day in nature have a 50% lower risk of mental health issues.
Disconnection

Dr. Mark Baez (Coahuiltecan Tribe) is the president of the Society for Indian Psychologists, whose clinic work focuses on adolescents and children. Baez told Native News Online that the issues driving the plummeting youth mental health are compounded in Native communities by the lasting effects of colonialism: poverty, generational trauma, geographic isolation, and loss of culture through federal campaigns to erase Native Americans.
“Many youth carry both online and historical trauma stressors simultaneously,” Baez said.
Those stressors, he said, result in a sense of isolation, antithetical to the core of many Native cultures and communities: connection.

“As clinicians, some of the signs that we see are loneliness, depression, anxiety, difficulty maintaining face-to-face relationships,” Baez said. “For Native youth, we see a lot of our kids on social media being digitally connected while simultaneously feeling disconnected from their family, community, culture, and peers.”

While putting down the phones and getting outside to play might be part of the solution, Native communities are seriously lacking in accessible, safe play spaces compared to other communities. An assessment of 237 playgrounds on or near tribal lands and urban areas with high Native populations found nearly 70% posed safety hazards, with varying degrees of repair and replacement needed.

Ashley Cornforth, Secretary-Treasurer for the Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux, told Native News Online building play spaces for youth can be part of a tribe’s stewardship of their land and seven-generations planning.

“We have a connection to our ancestral land,” she said. “We’re always going to be here. Play spaces are so integral to getting out and playing, and that physical activity has such a connection to mental health. How do we show that we want to maintain it? We want to make it stay good for our next youth.”
Screen Time

While the effects have been clear for many years, a 2021 Wall Street Journal investigation confirmed what many parents suspected: social media harms children’s mental health, and the tech giants behind the most popular apps are well aware. In recent years, Tribal Nations have filed suit against the social media companies , including Meta, Snap, ByteDance, and Alphabet, for their role in the youth mental health and suicide crisis plaguing Native communities. The suits point to addictive algorithms, gambling-like features, and exploitation of reciprocity.
On top of being designed to draw youth in over and over again, social media can provide ample opportunity for cruel bullying, far from the eyes of adults.

“We think, ‘just walk away, close the screen,’ right?” Baez said. “It’s easier said than done. The exposure to trauma and harmful content is very real: bullying, racism, lateral violence, misinformation. It has real harm.”

While the prevalence of screens in modern life may make screen time feel like an insurmountable obstacle for parents, both Baez and Cornforth said that healing Native youth and bringing them back to their culture starts with adults.

“If we want them to put their phones away, we need to do the same,” Baez said. “It sounds cliché, but kids are sponges, so lead by example. We need to create opportunities for youth to engage. Culture is prevention, and I go a step further: culture is medicine, because this culture is what has given us the ability to be resilient.”
