title: Cracks in the Universal Health Insurance system: An accounting of phase 1
content:
In the government’s telling, the first phase of the Universal Health Insurance rollout was a success . And with that success in hand, it says now that the scheme is ready to expand.

Six years ago, people in Port Said, Ismailia, Suez, South Sinai, Luxor and Aswan — the first governorates to see the rollout of the 2018 law  — were brought into the new system.

The promise was something better than the old model, a healthcare system built on social solidarity. People would pay less out of pocket. They would find a place in hospitals. Medicines and treatment would be there when they needed them.

But patients across those six governorates who spoke to Mada Masr over recent months describe months-long shortages of critical medicines and medical devices and appointment scheduling bottlenecks. Many, who were enrolled in the program whether they wanted to join or not, are now being effectively denied healthcare over unpaid insurance contributions that have climbed in some cases into the tens of thousands of pounds.

“All we hear is that the system is a success, but what we see is something completely different,” says a resident of Aswan. What is on the ground is a service well below even the minimum standard, he says.

The problems in the first phase were not unforeseen. Several officials and health policy experts involved in the drafting of the law at the time tell Mada Masr that the objections they raised nearly a decade ago remain at the heart of the challenges patients face today.

Nonetheless, the government is pressing ahead. While Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar says the government is preparing amendments to the law to address shortcomings that emerged during implementation, the state is already heavily promoting the second phase that will expand the scheme to another five governorates, starting with Minya, a heavily populated governorate with one of the highest poverty rates in the country.

Mada Masr spoke with health sector officials, specialist researchers, MPs and beneficiaries of the system to examine the main crises and challenges that emerged during the first phase, and whether they are now being carried into the scheme’s expansion.

One of the most common complaints patients living in the first-phase governorates raise is the shortage of medication.

For Mohamed Yasser, from Port Said, it was Budelizer, an inhaled medication used to treat asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. When his monthly prescription ran out, he was told the drug was unavailable through the scheme. It stayed that way for nearly six months.

During that time, Yasser had to buy the medication himself from private pharmacies, where the two boxes he needs each month cost around LE500 — even as he continued paying more than LE400 a month into the insurance scheme. Sometimes, he says, he could not find the medication or a substitute.

Getting medication through the system is itself consuming, Yasser explains. Patients must first book an appointment through the call center, then wait in a long queue at a family medicine clinic for a doctor to renew the prescription, before heading to the pharmacy, then to the cashier for the required fees and finally back to pick up the medication.

Every time, Yasser has to repeat the same process, which takes long hours, even though he is not seeking a medical examination but just renewing a prescription he takes regularly. Sometimes, there are no appointments available, and he is told to come back the following week, by which point he has already run out of the medicine. Other times, the doctor prescribes three packs, but the pharmacy dispenses only one because supplies are running low, forcing him to cut his dosage.

Because he kept having to cut back on the medication, his condition deteriorated, he says. Eventually, he filed a complaint with the Universal Health Insurance Authority demanding that the medication be made available again, noting that it had previously been dispensed routinely through the system before suddenly disappearing.

Khaled, an Al-Azhar school teacher in his mid-forties who lives in the Aboul Rish neighborhood in Aswan, has run into the same problem.

He depends on regular insulin injections and diabetes medication. Yet attempts to obtain them through his designated insurance hospital have repeatedly failed.

“They told me, ‘buy it from outside, when you get paid,’” he tells Mada Masr. Despite around LE800 being deducted from his salary every month in insurance contributions, he recently had to cover all of his treatment costs out of pocket. “I bought the insulin, eye drops, and also some vitamins, because none of them were available.”

Whenever Ahmed Yehia, an accountant from Luxor, accompanies his mother to collect her medication, they often leave empty-handed or with only part of the prescription, forcing him to buy the missing medicines from private pharmacies.

One of the drugs she regularly cannot obtain is Diamicron 60, used to treat type 2 diabetes. The two boxes she needs each month cost almost as much as the LE500 deducted from Yehia’s income in monthly insurance contributions.

He questions the point of paying into the insurance system if that is the case. “We are paying for nothing and getting no service,” he says.

Patients speaking to Mada Masr say access breaks down at almost every stage of the system. Even securing an appointment can take weeks, sometimes months.

In May, Khaled, the school teacher from Aswan, visited his insurance dental clinic while suffering from severe tooth pain. After waiting for hours to be seen, he was told to return two months later because the clinic “doesn’t have the specialist equipment.” With no other option, he paid LE1,400 for treatment at a private clinic.

Others describe the same pattern of delays. Mostafa, from Port Said, says he spent weeks trying to book a dental appointment. Every time he called, he was told there were no available slots. “I know people who book an appointment every week just in case they get sick. That’s an odd thing to do,” he says. “I’ve been trying for three weeks. Every time I go, they tell me the system is down.” At one point he asked for doctors to just prescribe medication instead of an appointment. “What can I do?” the staff replied, “The system is down.”

“All we hear is that the system is a success, but what we see is something completely different,” Khaled tells Mada Masr. The long waits for appointments, poor patient care from doctors and shortages of medicines and basic medical supplies all point to a service still well below even the minimum standard, he says.

For infants and young children who depend on specialist treatment, blocking access to medications carries a much higher risk.

Under the Universal Health Insurance system, families seeking insulin pumps, continuous glucose monitors or other high-cost treatments for their children are required to first obtain a court order. Even then, access is not guaranteed.

Some have responded by taking the authority itself to court. Ahmed Ibrahim, the father of Aisha, who filed a case before a Port Said administrative court seeking to compel the Universal Health Insurance Authority to provide Naglazyme, an enzyme replacement therapy. The authority had refused to cover the treatment despite his daughter’s diagnosis with mucopolysaccharidosis VI (MPS VI), or Maroteaux–Lamy syndrome , a rare sugar metabolic disorder, and medical reports issued by the Mansoura University Children’s Hospital and Egypt Healthcare Authority confirming that she needs it.

In a report on the case, a copy of which Mada Masr obtained, the State Commissioners Authority recommended that prior to the court issuing a final ruling, the Egyptian Forensic Medicine Authority must examine Aisha, determine whether the treatment is medically necessary and assess the appropriate dosage.

The report cites Article 18 of the Constitution and the 2018 Universal Health Insurance Law, both of which guarantee the right to healthcare and require the authority to finance treatment for insured patients. It also refers to established Supreme Administrative Court rulings holding that a public authority’s failure to take a decision required by law constitutes a negative administrative decision that can be challenged before the courts.

If medical necessity is established, the report concludes, the authority cannot justify withholding treatment simply because it falls outside its dispensing protocols. The constitutional and legal obligation to protect the rights to health and life, it says, takes precedence over administrative restrictions. Pending the forensic assessment, it provisionally recommended that the court overturn the authority’s refusal and require it to provide treatment.

Ahmed al-Desouky, another Port Said resident, filed a similar case in an effort to secure continued coverage for his nine-year-old daughter Mariam, who has lived with dermatomyositis, an autoimmune disease affecting the skin and muscles, for the past two and a half years. Her case is due to be heard on August 28.

Desouky says Mariam depends on intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG) infusions, a concentrated mix of antibodies, and Xeljanz, an enzyme inhibitor. In 2019, a course of the IVIG treatment cost LE18,000. She continued receiving the medication through the old health insurance system until Universal Health Insurance fully replaced it in 2021.

Today, he says, the treatment is theoretically dispensed every month. In practice, he is often told that the medication is unavailable within the system or that there is nowhere to obtain it.

Repeated delays in receiving the medications have caused his daughter’s condition to worsen. Lesions have spread across her body, and she is losing the ability to walk, he says.

Cases like Aisha’s and Mariam’s are emblematic of the system failures criticized in four parliamentary briefing requests MP Ahmed Farghaly submitted in April over the implementation of the Universal Health Insurance scheme in Port Said.

Addressed to the health and finance ministers and the head of the authority responsible for financing the system, the requests accuse the authority of treating healthcare as a commercial commodity, prioritizing costs over patient needs.

For Farghaly, children are among those paying the highest price. Under the previous system, he said, insulin pumps and glucose monitoring devices for newborns and children with diabetes were provided according to medical criteria. Under the Universal Health Insurance system, they are limited to families who obtain court orders or children already using the devices before the new scheme was introduced in their governorates.

Some families have already secured court rulings ordering the authority to provide them, yet the rulings have gone unenforced, according to Farghaly.

Children who are too young to recognize or communicate the symptoms of high blood sugar face severe health risks without the devices, he said.

The devices would cost the state only a few thousand pounds a month, Farghaly argued, while denying them can leave children in intensive care, ultimately driving up treatment costs for the state.

Farghaly said that the same logic extends beyond pediatric care. He accused the authority of replacing Prograf, the original immunosuppressant prescribed to kidney transplant patients, with the cheaper alternative Adport.

Around 150 transplant patients have been “neglected” as a result, he said. Having undergone cycles of dialysis and transplants in the hope of returning to normal lives, they were switched from Prograf to Adport several months prior, a change that, he said, has caused complications in some cases and left several patients hospitalized despite repeated warnings that the switch posed “a threat to their lives.”

His briefing requests also pointed to shortages in dialysis capacity. According to Farghaly, dozens of patients who require dialysis three times a week have been referred to private hospitals because insurance hospitals lack capacity. But under their contracts with the authority, private hospitals only provide dialysis sessions, leaving patients to pay out of pocket for medicines, follow-up tests and even blood transfusions when needed.

A former senior official at the health insurance authority says that telling a patient to “come back at the end of the month” just to book an appointment is “nonsense,” adding: “The maximum wait should be a week. If you’re telling patients to come back at the end of the month, then it means you don’t have enough doctors. And if there is a shortage of doctors, then that’s a big problem.”

Right to Medicine Foundation head Mahmoud Fouad questions the logic of charging such high insurance contributions under the scheme while failing to provide the promised services. “You can’t tell patients there is no medicine available when they are obliged to pay into the system,” he says. “If I’m using the service, I’m supposed to find it. It is not right that I receive only part of it.”

For some patients, the barrier begins before they see a doctor, before they pick up a prescription and before the system provides any care at all. It begins with a debt.

Five patients tell Mada Masr they discovered they have accumulated insurance contribution arrears only when they tried to access treatment. They all share one thing in common: unlike employees whose contributions are deducted automatically by their employers, they are personally responsible for paying their insurance contributions.

Mohamed, a grocery store worker in his mid-forties from Luxor and a father of two, enrolled in the Universal Health Insurance scheme in 2021 and received his insurance card, but he never used it.

Six months ago, he developed rheumatoid arthritis. As the pain worsened, he went to Luxor International Hospital, part of the Universal Health Insurance system, hoping to receive a biologic injection used to treat inflammatory arthritis — which costs around LE15,000 outside the scheme.

Instead, he says, he was told he owed the insurance system LE35,000.

“I was shocked. I don’t know what it’s for,” Mohamed tells Mada Masr. “I’ve never had a single examination. I activated the card and put it away. Suddenly, I owe money to the healthcare system that is supposed to be treating me.”

He then turned to the state’s Hayah Karima initiative for supporting people living in rural areas, hoping it could help cover the treatment. Instead, he was told he first needed to obtain a social insurance status printout. But securing that document requires him to clear the outstanding debts on his Universal Health Insurance account.

For now, Mohamed is surviving on painkillers, he says. “The pain is so severe, it’s unbearable. Even at my job in the grocery store, there are products I can’t lift anymore. Biologic therapy is the only solution.” But with his outstanding insurance debts, it remains out of reach.

Patients who cannot afford their contributions are meant to receive state support. According to Fouad, the Social Solidarity Ministry and the Universal Health Insurance Authority have signed a protocol to fund healthcare for people unable to pay. But what that support covers remains unclear.

The agreement does not specify how much funding is available, Fouad said, or even whether it only covers medical examinations or extends to treatment itself.

MPs have also questioned the scope of the funding, he added. To qualify, patients are required to obtain a “poverty certificate” proving financial hardship from the Social Solidarity Ministry before navigating a lengthy bureaucratic process involving multiple government offices, after which they are informed whether they qualify for assistance.

Yehia, the accountant from Luxor who works without a contract, has also run into a dead end. He owes around LE18,000 in Universal Health Insurance arrears. But attempts to resolve the issue have stalled because he has been told he must first obtain an insurance status printout from the social insurance authority, where he also has outstanding contributions, bringing what he owes the state to around LE40,000.

Cases like Mohamed’s and Yehia’s have become increasingly common over the past year, according to Mohamed Hassan Khalil, the coordinator of the Committee for the Defense of the Right to Health. Patients who seek treatment, he says, are instead confronted with insurance debts that can reach tens of thousands of pounds.

Rather than functioning as social health insurance, he argues, what is in place now is essentially a low-grade, compulsory commercial insurance scheme, where keeping up with payments becomes a condition for accessing care.

A former health insurance official who also served on the committee that drafted the Universal Health Insurance Law says the problem lies less with compulsory enrollment itself than how it is being implemented. People who have not used the service for years can find themselves confronted with large accumulated debts the moment they seek treatment, debts they were not aware were building up. They are only told about them once medical care becomes unavoidable, the former official explains.

Responding to questions about the growing contribution arrears, Health Ministry spokesperson Hossam Abdel Ghaffar tells Mada Masr that many people simply failed to register when they were supposed to.

“Out of consideration for the citizens’ circumstances, we have allowed installment plans, and we haven’t denied treatment even if someone owes money,” Abdel Ghaffar says. “Even so, there was not much interest, despite the fact that they can spread payments over several years. Even paying a single installment would show good faith.”

At the end of the day, he says, the system needs a sustainable funding mechanism.

Frustration with the scheme has driven many people to look for ways to avoid it altogether, after finding themselves required to pay monthly contributions without receiving the medicines or services they expected, Mohamed Senan from Qena says.

Some of Senan’s relatives and friends in Luxor have changed the addresses on their ID cards. By signing new rental contracts, they were able to register as residents of governorates where the insurance system has yet to be rolled out.

“We get nothing from the new system except deductions [from our income],” Senan says, arguing that the quality of care has not improved compared with the old health insurance system.

Mostafa, a 40-year-old father from Ismailia with muscular dystrophy, says he considered doing the same. He looked into changing his registered address to Sharqiya to leave the scheme. But he found that doing so required a registered rental contract and complicated administrative procedures. “I found it too difficult. It didn’t work,” he says.

Mostafa had gone to Salam hospital seeking an exemption from the LE250 monthly insurance contribution, explaining that his condition makes him unable to work.

“I was supposed to go get my insurance card. But instead they told me I owed LE11,000,” he says. “I asked, ‘What is that for?’ They said that once Universal Health Insurance started in the governorate, anyone whose ID says Ismailia was automatically enrolled.”

Hospital staff told him the system relies on civil registry records to determine who falls under the scheme.

“Why doesn’t anyone tell us we have to pay so we can avoid accumulating debt?” Mostafa asks.

Despite being unemployed due to his condition, staff told him that the minimum contribution is LE250, even for people without jobs. He showed them his integrated services card, a document issued by the Social Solidarity Ministry to people with disabilities. “They told me, ‘We don’t recognize that,’” he says. “How can the health insurance system not recognize a disability?”

They told Mostafa he needs to be enrolled in the Takaful and Karama program. “I’ve been trying to get onto it, but I still can’t,” he says.

Over the previous four decades, the public health insurance system expanded through a series of laws that extended coverage to different groups, repeatedly adjusting how the system was financed.

In 1964, the state established the country’s first national health insurance system. Law 75 covered government employees and Law 63 covered workers in public and private sectors insured under the Social Insurance Law. The two laws established the basic model of employer-to-employee contributions.

Another overhaul followed in 1975 with the passage of two laws that remain in force today. Law 32 reduced contribution rates for government employees and the government as the employer, but introduced payments that insured patients would pay when receiving healthcare services. Law 79 maintained higher contribution rates for public enterprise and formal private-sector workers,  without introducing the patient co-payments found in Law 32.

These differing arrangements reflected attempts to cope with the successive financial crises facing the health insurance system rather than a coherent strategy, health policy researchers Alaa Ghannam and Ahmed Azab tell Mada Masr.

As Egypt entered its open-door policy era, the healthcare system came under increasing strain. Out-of-pocket spending on medical care and medicines continued to rise, while public spending on health steadily declined, pushing large segments of the population, particularly poorer, marginalized and informally employed Egyptians, outside the reach of the public healthcare system, according to an article by Azab and Ghannam.

By the mid-1990s, policymakers had begun openly discussing comprehensive reform. And over the following decade, successive governments drafted new health insurance legislation, but none became law.

After the 2011 revolution, the draft law was extensively revised. The process gained new momentum following the adoption of the 2014 Constitution, which committed the state to establishing a comprehensive health insurance system. A committee bringing together government officials, health policy experts and civil society groups spent the following years debating and revising the draft, presenting it across numerous sessions to the National Social Dialogue before completing its work in 2016.

In 2017, the Health Ministry, whose head chaired the committee, submitted the Universal Health Insurance bill to Parliament.

While previous attempts had dragged on for decades, the final push moved with speed. The bill was passed in 2018 and signed into law by the president.

The law was intended to resolve many of the structural problems by replacing the patchwork of insurance schemes with a unified national system, covering all Egyptian citizens residing in the country.

The law envisions a gradual nationwide rollout over 13 years, divided into six geographical phases.

Unlike the previous health insurance system, which covered specific categories of formal-sector workers, the Universal Health Insurance scheme is financed through mandatory contributions paid by all citizens. The contributions are deducted directly from incomes in a system akin to taxation.

Employees continue to contribute one percent of their salary, as was the case before, but the new law also requires an additional three percent for a spouse and one percent for each child. Landowners, business owners and self-employed professionals pay five percent of either their insured income or their taxable income, whichever is higher.

Access to healthcare under the scheme is contingent on remaining up to date with contributions. Those who fall behind on payments must settle their arrears — either in full or through installments — before they can access services, except in emergency cases.

On paper, the system represented a fundamental redesign of how healthcare would be financed and delivered. But according to people involved in drafting the law, the first phase began before many of its basic requirements were in place.

Ahead of the launch in Port Said in 2019, then-Health Minister Ahmed Emad and the head of the health insurance authority at the time, Ali Hegazy, publicly maintained that everything was ready for implementation. But once it began, it quickly became clear that key elements were missing, including healthcare infrastructure and sufficient medical staff.

Fouad says that during parliamentary debates over the bill, Hegazy presented “inaccurate” figures on the number of hospitals and expected beneficiaries in the first-phase governorates. Mohamed al-Ammary, then-chair of Parliament’s Health Committee, challenged those figures, saying they did not match data his committee had received from the Health Ministry and required further verification.

The discrepancies ultimately led to the dismissal of Hegazy and Ammary from their posts, says Ghannam, who served on the committee that drafted the law.

The former senior official, a fellow committee member, says they opposed creating an entirely new health insurance system from the outset.

“I believed the old system needed reform, including for its funding resources, but, instead, they decided to build a completely new system,” they say. “That’s already a very difficult undertaking.” Fixing the flaws in the existing system and improving the quality of healthcare would have been far less costly, they argue.

They say they raised these concerns before the law was passed, including in a meeting with Ammary . “My objections were clear. The priority should have been the segments most in need — women breadwinners and informal workers. You have 20 million people who need meaningful services and improved budget and contribution sources.”

In their view, the old system’s biggest weakness was its financing.

“In 2014, for example, total funding was around LE5 billion, and it covered more than 50 million people. Each citizen was contributing LE100 a year. That’s a very small amount. The state doesn’t finance health insurance. It is financed through contributions. So if the average is only LE100, of course there will be gaps in services.”

While the new scheme appears designed to address underfunding by pooling mandatory contributions from a much broader share of the population, it does so by shifting more of the burden onto citizens.

Khalil, the coordinator of the Committee for the Defense of the Right to Health, argues that the shift is part of the state’s gradual retreat from its role in financing healthcare. Under the new system, healthcare is treated as a paid service rather than a right guaranteed by the state, he says.

As a result, access to care becomes tied to people’s ability to pay rather than membership in a solidarity-based society that is supposed to protect everyone, Khalil adds.

He also notes that so far, the public has no visibility into how the system’s finances are managed, although the law requires its budget to be presented to Parliament and published, thereby allowing for an understanding of the size of the financial surplus and how it is being used.

Ghannam agrees that the previous insurance system had become unsustainable after decades of limited coverage, low contributions and deteriorating services. It also lacked proper governance, he says, because the same institution both delivered healthcare and monitored its own performance. Many insured Egyptians avoided using it altogether, opting instead to pay private providers, he adds.

But unlike the former official, Ghannam believes the idea of a universal health insurance system is sound in principle. In his view, the problem lies in how it has been implemented.

A nationwide reform on this scale should have begun with a comprehensive implementation plan, Ghannam says. Instead, he argues, the rollout started before such a plan existed, without adequate infrastructure or sufficient resources, because there was political pressure to produce an “achievement.”

This should have never happened, particularly given that those resources are ultimately being collected from citizens themselves, he adds.

At a meeting chaired by Prime Minister Mostafa Madbuly in May, the government said it is working on amendments to the 2018 law intended to overhaul the scheme’s governance, improve coordination between its bodies, strengthen its financial resources and address shortcomings that have emerged during implementation.

Yet officials presented those changes as refinements to what they say was otherwise a successful first phase.

Ehab Abu Eish, the deputy chair of the Universal Health Insurance Authority, said during the meeting that the scheme has so far enrolled around 5.4 million beneficiaries across the six governorates where it has been introduced, representing 83.6 percent of the target population. Around 16 percent of those enrolled are classified as unable to pay, he said at the time, describing this as evidence of the scheme’s social and humanitarian role in providing healthcare to those who need it the most.

Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said in June that around 82 percent of beneficiaries are “satisfied with the services” they receive, which he described as consistent with international benchmarks.

According to Fouad, there is a lot of hype surrounding the scheme. “Officials keep citing figures — 35 million services in Ismailia, 35 million services in Aswan.”

He argues that officials often inflate those figures by counting administrative procedures as healthcare services. They consider registering online or giving someone a service number to be a “service” in itself, he says. “If I go to see a specialist and they refer me to a consultant, that is considered a service. And that is just marketing.”

What really matters, he stresses, “is whether we get treatment, and all the treatment we need, or not.”

The experiences of patients who spoke to Mada Masr across the first-phase governorates and the information and figures cited in Farghaly’s briefing requests show that the answer for many remains: no, compulsory enrollment has not translated into guaranteed treatment.

The government nevertheless is moving ahead. Madbuly confirmed the government is now preparing for the second phase, which will extend the scheme to Minya, Damietta, North Sinai and Kafr al-Sheikh, adding around 12 million people to the system.

Last year, the government even considered adding Alexandria to the second phase, despite having yet to present Parliament with “an accounting of the first phase,” Fouad told Mada Masr at the time.

Ghannam hopes the problems that plagued the launch in Port Said will not be repeated as the second phase begins in Minya, the first governorate in the new rollout. Repeating the same mistakes there would carry far greater consequences because of Minya’s much larger population.

Minya also has one of the highest rates of poverty across Egypt’s governorates, meaning the state treasury will have to shoulder a greater share of the cost of covering low-income residents, he says. Its predominantly rural population also makes the readiness of primary healthcare units and the availability of family physicians especially important.

“What happens when all 100 million Egyptians are brought into the system?” the former official asks. “What will it look like then?”

contentBlocks.text: In the government’s telling, the first phase of the Universal Health Insurance rollout was a success . And with that success in hand, it says now that the scheme is ready to expand.
Six years ago, people in Port Said, Ismailia, Suez, South Sinai, Luxor and Aswan — the first governorates to see the rollout of the 2018 law  — were brought into the new system.

The promise was something better than the old model, a healthcare system built on social solidarity. People would pay less out of pocket. They would find a place in hospitals. Medicines and treatment would be there when they needed them.

But patients across those six governorates who spoke to Mada Masr over recent months describe months-long shortages of critical medicines and medical devices and appointment scheduling bottlenecks. Many, who were enrolled in the program whether they wanted to join or not, are now being effectively denied healthcare over unpaid insurance contributions that have climbed in some cases into the tens of thousands of pounds.

“All we hear is that the system is a success, but what we see is something completely different,” says a resident of Aswan. What is on the ground is a service well below even the minimum standard, he says.

The problems in the first phase were not unforeseen. Several officials and health policy experts involved in the drafting of the law at the time tell Mada Masr that the objections they raised nearly a decade ago remain at the heart of the challenges patients face today.

Nonetheless, the government is pressing ahead. While Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar says the government is preparing amendments to the law to address shortcomings that emerged during implementation, the state is already heavily promoting the second phase that will expand the scheme to another five governorates, starting with Minya, a heavily populated governorate with one of the highest poverty rates in the country.

Mada Masr spoke with health sector officials, specialist researchers, MPs and beneficiaries of the system to examine the main crises and challenges that emerged during the first phase, and whether they are now being carried into the scheme’s expansion.
One of the most common complaints patients living in the first-phase governorates raise is the shortage of medication.

For Mohamed Yasser, from Port Said, it was Budelizer, an inhaled medication used to treat asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. When his monthly prescription ran out, he was told the drug was unavailable through the scheme. It stayed that way for nearly six months.

During that time, Yasser had to buy the medication himself from private pharmacies, where the two boxes he needs each month cost around LE500 — even as he continued paying more than LE400 a month into the insurance scheme. Sometimes, he says, he could not find the medication or a substitute.

Getting medication through the system is itself consuming, Yasser explains. Patients must first book an appointment through the call center, then wait in a long queue at a family medicine clinic for a doctor to renew the prescription, before heading to the pharmacy, then to the cashier for the required fees and finally back to pick up the medication.

Every time, Yasser has to repeat the same process, which takes long hours, even though he is not seeking a medical examination but just renewing a prescription he takes regularly. Sometimes, there are no appointments available, and he is told to come back the following week, by which point he has already run out of the medicine. Other times, the doctor prescribes three packs, but the pharmacy dispenses only one because supplies are running low, forcing him to cut his dosage.

Because he kept having to cut back on the medication, his condition deteriorated, he says. Eventually, he filed a complaint with the Universal Health Insurance Authority demanding that the medication be made available again, noting that it had previously been dispensed routinely through the system before suddenly disappearing.
Khaled, an Al-Azhar school teacher in his mid-forties who lives in the Aboul Rish neighborhood in Aswan, has run into the same problem.
He depends on regular insulin injections and diabetes medication. Yet attempts to obtain them through his designated insurance hospital have repeatedly failed.

“They told me, ‘buy it from outside, when you get paid,’” he tells Mada Masr. Despite around LE800 being deducted from his salary every month in insurance contributions, he recently had to cover all of his treatment costs out of pocket. “I bought the insulin, eye drops, and also some vitamins, because none of them were available.”

Whenever Ahmed Yehia, an accountant from Luxor, accompanies his mother to collect her medication, they often leave empty-handed or with only part of the prescription, forcing him to buy the missing medicines from private pharmacies.

One of the drugs she regularly cannot obtain is Diamicron 60, used to treat type 2 diabetes. The two boxes she needs each month cost almost as much as the LE500 deducted from Yehia’s income in monthly insurance contributions.
He questions the point of paying into the insurance system if that is the case. “We are paying for nothing and getting no service,” he says.
Patients speaking to Mada Masr say access breaks down at almost every stage of the system. Even securing an appointment can take weeks, sometimes months.

In May, Khaled, the school teacher from Aswan, visited his insurance dental clinic while suffering from severe tooth pain. After waiting for hours to be seen, he was told to return two months later because the clinic “doesn’t have the specialist equipment.” With no other option, he paid LE1,400 for treatment at a private clinic.

Others describe the same pattern of delays. Mostafa, from Port Said, says he spent weeks trying to book a dental appointment. Every time he called, he was told there were no available slots. “I know people who book an appointment every week just in case they get sick. That’s an odd thing to do,” he says. “I’ve been trying for three weeks. Every time I go, they tell me the system is down.” At one point he asked for doctors to just prescribe medication instead of an appointment. “What can I do?” the staff replied, “The system is down.”

“All we hear is that the system is a success, but what we see is something completely different,” Khaled tells Mada Masr. The long waits for appointments, poor patient care from doctors and shortages of medicines and basic medical supplies all point to a service still well below even the minimum standard, he says.
For infants and young children who depend on specialist treatment, blocking access to medications carries a much higher risk.

Under the Universal Health Insurance system, families seeking insulin pumps, continuous glucose monitors or other high-cost treatments for their children are required to first obtain a court order. Even then, access is not guaranteed.

Some have responded by taking the authority itself to court. Ahmed Ibrahim, the father of Aisha, who filed a case before a Port Said administrative court seeking to compel the Universal Health Insurance Authority to provide Naglazyme, an enzyme replacement therapy. The authority had refused to cover the treatment despite his daughter’s diagnosis with mucopolysaccharidosis VI (MPS VI), or Maroteaux–Lamy syndrome , a rare sugar metabolic disorder, and medical reports issued by the Mansoura University Children’s Hospital and Egypt Healthcare Authority confirming that she needs it.

In a report on the case, a copy of which Mada Masr obtained, the State Commissioners Authority recommended that prior to the court issuing a final ruling, the Egyptian Forensic Medicine Authority must examine Aisha, determine whether the treatment is medically necessary and assess the appropriate dosage.

The report cites Article 18 of the Constitution and the 2018 Universal Health Insurance Law, both of which guarantee the right to healthcare and require the authority to finance treatment for insured patients. It also refers to established Supreme Administrative Court rulings holding that a public authority’s failure to take a decision required by law constitutes a negative administrative decision that can be challenged before the courts.

If medical necessity is established, the report concludes, the authority cannot justify withholding treatment simply because it falls outside its dispensing protocols. The constitutional and legal obligation to protect the rights to health and life, it says, takes precedence over administrative restrictions. Pending the forensic assessment, it provisionally recommended that the court overturn the authority’s refusal and require it to provide treatment.

Ahmed al-Desouky, another Port Said resident, filed a similar case in an effort to secure continued coverage for his nine-year-old daughter Mariam, who has lived with dermatomyositis, an autoimmune disease affecting the skin and muscles, for the past two and a half years. Her case is due to be heard on August 28.

Desouky says Mariam depends on intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG) infusions, a concentrated mix of antibodies, and Xeljanz, an enzyme inhibitor. In 2019, a course of the IVIG treatment cost LE18,000. She continued receiving the medication through the old health insurance system until Universal Health Insurance fully replaced it in 2021.
Today, he says, the treatment is theoretically dispensed every month. In practice, he is often told that the medication is unavailable within the system or that there is nowhere to obtain it.
Repeated delays in receiving the medications have caused his daughter’s condition to worsen. Lesions have spread across her body, and she is losing the ability to walk, he says.

Cases like Aisha’s and Mariam’s are emblematic of the system failures criticized in four parliamentary briefing requests MP Ahmed Farghaly submitted in April over the implementation of the Universal Health Insurance scheme in Port Said.

Addressed to the health and finance ministers and the head of the authority responsible for financing the system, the requests accuse the authority of treating healthcare as a commercial commodity, prioritizing costs over patient needs.

For Farghaly, children are among those paying the highest price. Under the previous system, he said, insulin pumps and glucose monitoring devices for newborns and children with diabetes were provided according to medical criteria. Under the Universal Health Insurance system, they are limited to families who obtain court orders or children already using the devices before the new scheme was introduced in their governorates.
Some families have already secured court rulings ordering the authority to provide them, yet the rulings have gone unenforced, according to Farghaly.
Children who are too young to recognize or communicate the symptoms of high blood sugar face severe health risks without the devices, he said.
The devices would cost the state only a few thousand pounds a month, Farghaly argued, while denying them can leave children in intensive care, ultimately driving up treatment costs for the state.

Farghaly said that the same logic extends beyond pediatric care. He accused the authority of replacing Prograf, the original immunosuppressant prescribed to kidney transplant patients, with the cheaper alternative Adport.

Around 150 transplant patients have been “neglected” as a result, he said. Having undergone cycles of dialysis and transplants in the hope of returning to normal lives, they were switched from Prograf to Adport several months prior, a change that, he said, has caused complications in some cases and left several patients hospitalized despite repeated warnings that the switch posed “a threat to their lives.”

His briefing requests also pointed to shortages in dialysis capacity. According to Farghaly, dozens of patients who require dialysis three times a week have been referred to private hospitals because insurance hospitals lack capacity. But under their contracts with the authority, private hospitals only provide dialysis sessions, leaving patients to pay out of pocket for medicines, follow-up tests and even blood transfusions when needed.

A former senior official at the health insurance authority says that telling a patient to “come back at the end of the month” just to book an appointment is “nonsense,” adding: “The maximum wait should be a week. If you’re telling patients to come back at the end of the month, then it means you don’t have enough doctors. And if there is a shortage of doctors, then that’s a big problem.”

Right to Medicine Foundation head Mahmoud Fouad questions the logic of charging such high insurance contributions under the scheme while failing to provide the promised services. “You can’t tell patients there is no medicine available when they are obliged to pay into the system,” he says. “If I’m using the service, I’m supposed to find it. It is not right that I receive only part of it.”
For some patients, the barrier begins before they see a doctor, before they pick up a prescription and before the system provides any care at all. It begins with a debt.

Five patients tell Mada Masr they discovered they have accumulated insurance contribution arrears only when they tried to access treatment. They all share one thing in common: unlike employees whose contributions are deducted automatically by their employers, they are personally responsible for paying their insurance contributions.
Mohamed, a grocery store worker in his mid-forties from Luxor and a father of two, enrolled in the Universal Health Insurance scheme in 2021 and received his insurance card, but he never used it.

Six months ago, he developed rheumatoid arthritis. As the pain worsened, he went to Luxor International Hospital, part of the Universal Health Insurance system, hoping to receive a biologic injection used to treat inflammatory arthritis — which costs around LE15,000 outside the scheme.
Instead, he says, he was told he owed the insurance system LE35,000.

“I was shocked. I don’t know what it’s for,” Mohamed tells Mada Masr. “I’ve never had a single examination. I activated the card and put it away. Suddenly, I owe money to the healthcare system that is supposed to be treating me.”

He then turned to the state’s Hayah Karima initiative for supporting people living in rural areas, hoping it could help cover the treatment. Instead, he was told he first needed to obtain a social insurance status printout. But securing that document requires him to clear the outstanding debts on his Universal Health Insurance account.

For now, Mohamed is surviving on painkillers, he says. “The pain is so severe, it’s unbearable. Even at my job in the grocery store, there are products I can’t lift anymore. Biologic therapy is the only solution.” But with his outstanding insurance debts, it remains out of reach.

Patients who cannot afford their contributions are meant to receive state support. According to Fouad, the Social Solidarity Ministry and the Universal Health Insurance Authority have signed a protocol to fund healthcare for people unable to pay. But what that support covers remains unclear.
The agreement does not specify how much funding is available, Fouad said, or even whether it only covers medical examinations or extends to treatment itself.

MPs have also questioned the scope of the funding, he added. To qualify, patients are required to obtain a “poverty certificate” proving financial hardship from the Social Solidarity Ministry before navigating a lengthy bureaucratic process involving multiple government offices, after which they are informed whether they qualify for assistance.

Yehia, the accountant from Luxor who works without a contract, has also run into a dead end. He owes around LE18,000 in Universal Health Insurance arrears. But attempts to resolve the issue have stalled because he has been told he must first obtain an insurance status printout from the social insurance authority, where he also has outstanding contributions, bringing what he owes the state to around LE40,000.

Cases like Mohamed’s and Yehia’s have become increasingly common over the past year, according to Mohamed Hassan Khalil, the coordinator of the Committee for the Defense of the Right to Health. Patients who seek treatment, he says, are instead confronted with insurance debts that can reach tens of thousands of pounds.

Rather than functioning as social health insurance, he argues, what is in place now is essentially a low-grade, compulsory commercial insurance scheme, where keeping up with payments becomes a condition for accessing care.

A former health insurance official who also served on the committee that drafted the Universal Health Insurance Law says the problem lies less with compulsory enrollment itself than how it is being implemented. People who have not used the service for years can find themselves confronted with large accumulated debts the moment they seek treatment, debts they were not aware were building up. They are only told about them once medical care becomes unavoidable, the former official explains.

Responding to questions about the growing contribution arrears, Health Ministry spokesperson Hossam Abdel Ghaffar tells Mada Masr that many people simply failed to register when they were supposed to.

“Out of consideration for the citizens’ circumstances, we have allowed installment plans, and we haven’t denied treatment even if someone owes money,” Abdel Ghaffar says. “Even so, there was not much interest, despite the fact that they can spread payments over several years. Even paying a single installment would show good faith.”
At the end of the day, he says, the system needs a sustainable funding mechanism.

Frustration with the scheme has driven many people to look for ways to avoid it altogether, after finding themselves required to pay monthly contributions without receiving the medicines or services they expected, Mohamed Senan from Qena says.

Some of Senan’s relatives and friends in Luxor have changed the addresses on their ID cards. By signing new rental contracts, they were able to register as residents of governorates where the insurance system has yet to be rolled out.
“We get nothing from the new system except deductions [from our income],” Senan says, arguing that the quality of care has not improved compared with the old health insurance system.

Mostafa, a 40-year-old father from Ismailia with muscular dystrophy, says he considered doing the same. He looked into changing his registered address to Sharqiya to leave the scheme. But he found that doing so required a registered rental contract and complicated administrative procedures. “I found it too difficult. It didn’t work,” he says.
Mostafa had gone to Salam hospital seeking an exemption from the LE250 monthly insurance contribution, explaining that his condition makes him unable to work.

“I was supposed to go get my insurance card. But instead they told me I owed LE11,000,” he says. “I asked, ‘What is that for?’ They said that once Universal Health Insurance started in the governorate, anyone whose ID says Ismailia was automatically enrolled.”
Hospital staff told him the system relies on civil registry records to determine who falls under the scheme.
“Why doesn’t anyone tell us we have to pay so we can avoid accumulating debt?” Mostafa asks.

Despite being unemployed due to his condition, staff told him that the minimum contribution is LE250, even for people without jobs. He showed them his integrated services card, a document issued by the Social Solidarity Ministry to people with disabilities. “They told me, ‘We don’t recognize that,’” he says. “How can the health insurance system not recognize a disability?”
They told Mostafa he needs to be enrolled in the Takaful and Karama program. “I’ve been trying to get onto it, but I still can’t,” he says.
Over the previous four decades, the public health insurance system expanded through a series of laws that extended coverage to different groups, repeatedly adjusting how the system was financed.

In 1964, the state established the country’s first national health insurance system. Law 75 covered government employees and Law 63 covered workers in public and private sectors insured under the Social Insurance Law. The two laws established the basic model of employer-to-employee contributions.

Another overhaul followed in 1975 with the passage of two laws that remain in force today. Law 32 reduced contribution rates for government employees and the government as the employer, but introduced payments that insured patients would pay when receiving healthcare services. Law 79 maintained higher contribution rates for public enterprise and formal private-sector workers,  without introducing the patient co-payments found in Law 32.

These differing arrangements reflected attempts to cope with the successive financial crises facing the health insurance system rather than a coherent strategy, health policy researchers Alaa Ghannam and Ahmed Azab tell Mada Masr.

As Egypt entered its open-door policy era, the healthcare system came under increasing strain. Out-of-pocket spending on medical care and medicines continued to rise, while public spending on health steadily declined, pushing large segments of the population, particularly poorer, marginalized and informally employed Egyptians, outside the reach of the public healthcare system, according to an article by Azab and Ghannam.
By the mid-1990s, policymakers had begun openly discussing comprehensive reform. And over the following decade, successive governments drafted new health insurance legislation, but none became law.

After the 2011 revolution, the draft law was extensively revised. The process gained new momentum following the adoption of the 2014 Constitution, which committed the state to establishing a comprehensive health insurance system. A committee bringing together government officials, health policy experts and civil society groups spent the following years debating and revising the draft, presenting it across numerous sessions to the National Social Dialogue before completing its work in 2016.
In 2017, the Health Ministry, whose head chaired the committee, submitted the Universal Health Insurance bill to Parliament.
While previous attempts had dragged on for decades, the final push moved with speed. The bill was passed in 2018 and signed into law by the president.
The law was intended to resolve many of the structural problems by replacing the patchwork of insurance schemes with a unified national system, covering all Egyptian citizens residing in the country.
The law envisions a gradual nationwide rollout over 13 years, divided into six geographical phases.

Unlike the previous health insurance system, which covered specific categories of formal-sector workers, the Universal Health Insurance scheme is financed through mandatory contributions paid by all citizens. The contributions are deducted directly from incomes in a system akin to taxation.

Employees continue to contribute one percent of their salary, as was the case before, but the new law also requires an additional three percent for a spouse and one percent for each child. Landowners, business owners and self-employed professionals pay five percent of either their insured income or their taxable income, whichever is higher.

Access to healthcare under the scheme is contingent on remaining up to date with contributions. Those who fall behind on payments must settle their arrears — either in full or through installments — before they can access services, except in emergency cases.

On paper, the system represented a fundamental redesign of how healthcare would be financed and delivered. But according to people involved in drafting the law, the first phase began before many of its basic requirements were in place.

Ahead of the launch in Port Said in 2019, then-Health Minister Ahmed Emad and the head of the health insurance authority at the time, Ali Hegazy, publicly maintained that everything was ready for implementation. But once it began, it quickly became clear that key elements were missing, including healthcare infrastructure and sufficient medical staff.

Fouad says that during parliamentary debates over the bill, Hegazy presented “inaccurate” figures on the number of hospitals and expected beneficiaries in the first-phase governorates. Mohamed al-Ammary, then-chair of Parliament’s Health Committee, challenged those figures, saying they did not match data his committee had received from the Health Ministry and required further verification.
The discrepancies ultimately led to the dismissal of Hegazy and Ammary from their posts, says Ghannam, who served on the committee that drafted the law.
The former senior official, a fellow committee member, says they opposed creating an entirely new health insurance system from the outset.

“I believed the old system needed reform, including for its funding resources, but, instead, they decided to build a completely new system,” they say. “That’s already a very difficult undertaking.” Fixing the flaws in the existing system and improving the quality of healthcare would have been far less costly, they argue.

They say they raised these concerns before the law was passed, including in a meeting with Ammary . “My objections were clear. The priority should have been the segments most in need — women breadwinners and informal workers. You have 20 million people who need meaningful services and improved budget and contribution sources.”
In their view, the old system’s biggest weakness was its financing.

“In 2014, for example, total funding was around LE5 billion, and it covered more than 50 million people. Each citizen was contributing LE100 a year. That’s a very small amount. The state doesn’t finance health insurance. It is financed through contributions. So if the average is only LE100, of course there will be gaps in services.”
While the new scheme appears designed to address underfunding by pooling mandatory contributions from a much broader share of the population, it does so by shifting more of the burden onto citizens.

Khalil, the coordinator of the Committee for the Defense of the Right to Health, argues that the shift is part of the state’s gradual retreat from its role in financing healthcare. Under the new system, healthcare is treated as a paid service rather than a right guaranteed by the state, he says.
As a result, access to care becomes tied to people’s ability to pay rather than membership in a solidarity-based society that is supposed to protect everyone, Khalil adds.

He also notes that so far, the public has no visibility into how the system’s finances are managed, although the law requires its budget to be presented to Parliament and published, thereby allowing for an understanding of the size of the financial surplus and how it is being used.

Ghannam agrees that the previous insurance system had become unsustainable after decades of limited coverage, low contributions and deteriorating services. It also lacked proper governance, he says, because the same institution both delivered healthcare and monitored its own performance. Many insured Egyptians avoided using it altogether, opting instead to pay private providers, he adds.
But unlike the former official, Ghannam believes the idea of a universal health insurance system is sound in principle. In his view, the problem lies in how it has been implemented.

A nationwide reform on this scale should have begun with a comprehensive implementation plan, Ghannam says. Instead, he argues, the rollout started before such a plan existed, without adequate infrastructure or sufficient resources, because there was political pressure to produce an “achievement.”
This should have never happened, particularly given that those resources are ultimately being collected from citizens themselves, he adds.

At a meeting chaired by Prime Minister Mostafa Madbuly in May, the government said it is working on amendments to the 2018 law intended to overhaul the scheme’s governance, improve coordination between its bodies, strengthen its financial resources and address shortcomings that have emerged during implementation.
Yet officials presented those changes as refinements to what they say was otherwise a successful first phase.

Ehab Abu Eish, the deputy chair of the Universal Health Insurance Authority, said during the meeting that the scheme has so far enrolled around 5.4 million beneficiaries across the six governorates where it has been introduced, representing 83.6 percent of the target population. Around 16 percent of those enrolled are classified as unable to pay, he said at the time, describing this as evidence of the scheme’s social and humanitarian role in providing healthcare to those who need it the most.

Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said in June that around 82 percent of beneficiaries are “satisfied with the services” they receive, which he described as consistent with international benchmarks.
According to Fouad, there is a lot of hype surrounding the scheme. “Officials keep citing figures — 35 million services in Ismailia, 35 million services in Aswan.”

He argues that officials often inflate those figures by counting administrative procedures as healthcare services. They consider registering online or giving someone a service number to be a “service” in itself, he says. “If I go to see a specialist and they refer me to a consultant, that is considered a service. And that is just marketing.”
What really matters, he stresses, “is whether we get treatment, and all the treatment we need, or not.”

The experiences of patients who spoke to Mada Masr across the first-phase governorates and the information and figures cited in Farghaly’s briefing requests show that the answer for many remains: no, compulsory enrollment has not translated into guaranteed treatment.

The government nevertheless is moving ahead. Madbuly confirmed the government is now preparing for the second phase, which will extend the scheme to Minya, Damietta, North Sinai and Kafr al-Sheikh, adding around 12 million people to the system.
Last year, the government even considered adding Alexandria to the second phase, despite having yet to present Parliament with “an accounting of the first phase,” Fouad told Mada Masr at the time.

Ghannam hopes the problems that plagued the launch in Port Said will not be repeated as the second phase begins in Minya, the first governorate in the new rollout. Repeating the same mistakes there would carry far greater consequences because of Minya’s much larger population.

Minya also has one of the highest rates of poverty across Egypt’s governorates, meaning the state treasury will have to shoulder a greater share of the cost of covering low-income residents, he says. Its predominantly rural population also makes the readiness of primary healthcare units and the availability of family physicians especially important.
For Ghannam, Minya may prove the scheme’s first real test. But bigger challenges lie ahead.
“What happens when all 100 million Egyptians are brought into the system?” the former official asks. “What will it look like then?”

title: Trump Medicaid Rule Could Strip Coverage From Seriously Ill People
content:
Even terminally ill people must prove they are too sick to work to keep their Medicaid coverage.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Afew weeks ago, we argued the Trump administration was seeking to invent new ways to punish Americans . The idea was that the authoritarian impulses of the MAGA-run government will need to dial up the cruelty in order to sow chaos and pave the way for a broader assault on democracy.

Well, this week a rule was issued by Medicare and Medicaid services that shows just how proficient the Trump administration is at inflicting pain. And the consequences for poor, seriously ill Americans could be devastating.

Before we explain the rule, it’s worth contemplating the often destructive role healthcare — both the lack of it and exorbitant costs associated with it — play in the lives of working-class Americans.

Poll after poll shows that working people rank anxiety over healthcare costs at the top of the list of high-priority concerns . Unpaid medical bills are the most likely cause of personal bankruptcy in the US. Unlike any other wealthy nation on earth, when Americans lose their jobs, they often lose access to a doctor as well.

The US healthcare system is already inherently extractive — making it even more prohibitively expensive means more people will suffer with diseases that can be cured and die from afflictions that would otherwise be treatable. All of this makes the working class vulnerable and likewise incapable of asserting their right to be healthy.

And that’s where the new rule comes in.

The government agency that administers Medicaid has created a new criterion, ‘medically frail,’ which must be met to qualify for the program without working — even if you only have weeks to live. It didn’t exist prior to the passage of the Big Beautiful Bill.

Before that landmark legislation was signed into law, Medicaid was primarily a means-tested program, accessible to those with low enough incomes to qualify. But the new rule means even if you have pancreatic cancer, HIV, or Parkinson’s, you will have to meet work requirements to maintain eligibility, or prove you are too sick to comply. Your doctor’s opinion won’t matter. It will be up to the bureaucrats.

Essentially, this amounts to navigating a process fashioned explicitly to kick people off the program. That means filling out forms and filing papers and hoping someone sitting at a desk determines you comply with a definition critics say is vaguely written and open to interpretation.

This is all part of a scheme hatched during the passage of the massively destructive Big Beautiful Bill last year. Trump and his MAGA cohorts wanted to give a trillion-dollar tax break to the top one percent. But the cuts were projected to add trillions to an already historically high federal debt.

So, to conjure a so-called “pay for,” Republicans turned to Medicaid, the critical program that provides healthcare to the poorest Americans.

Simply slashing funding was politically unpalatable, even for the party best known for trying to dismantle Obamacare multiple times without providing a viable alternative. So Republicans came up with a workaround: make it more difficult to qualify.

In practice, that translated into the aforementioned new work requirements.

The medical frailty rule shows, in part, how this overarching plan will lead to fewer beneficiaries: create a complicated bureaucracy difficult to navigate, then cut people who can’t comply.

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office projects the additional work rules will lead to 11.8 million people dropping Medicaid over the next decade — 7 million of whom they project will not find insurance elsewhere.

And it won’t be millions of idle young men playing video games and refusing to work who are affected by the new rules, as House Speaker Mike Johnson suggested. Instead, as the CBO concludes, the burdensome paperwork and subjective standards will lead to most people simply dropping out, whether they qualify or not.

Democrats are pushing back hard against the regulation. In a letter to the Health and Human Services secretary, a group of Connecticut representatives argued that the rule exceeded the intent of the law.

“The overwhelming impact of this rule is that eligible citizens will be denied Medicaid coverage, states will expend unacceptable resources processing complex paperwork, safety-net providers will be further burdened, and population health will decline,” wrote Democratic Reps. John Larson, Joe Courtney, Rosa DeLauro, Jim Himes, and Jahana Hayes.

On the House floor, Courtney said vague standards and arbitrary rules would create confusion for critically ill people without care.

“The hope was that a medical diagnosis for cancer or HIV or other serious chronic conditions would qualify for protection. Instead the rule makes clear that a cancer diagnosis will not automatically qualify for an exception. Instead the patient will have to document that the disease actually impairs their ability to work,” he said.

“This rule will create chaos and dramatically increase the number of desperately ill people who will lose their coverage.”

We reached out to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, the agency that administers both programs. They have yet to respond.

In the meantime, if you’re skeptical that work requirements are mostly aimed at reducing the number of people on Medicaid, consider what’s happening with the federal government’s primary program for distributing food aid to low-income families.

Known as SNAP, or Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, it’s been a frequent target for Republicans, who argue it’s rife with fraud and abuse. Those claims are exaggerated or unfounded — but, again, the Big Beautiful Bill imposed work requirements, and the consequences have been catastrophic.

A recent New York Times article reported that since the new paperwork requirements for SNAP were instituted in Arizona, nearly 440,000 recipients have lost assistance. The piece recounts how the bureaucratic demands are so extreme that some beneficiaries have been asked to provide documentation of money obtained from panhandling.

If this is what people receiving SNAP benefits have been subjected to, imagine what’s going to happen to people who will need to navigate the new Medicare requirements while struggling with a debilitating or terminal illness.

The point is that the same burdensome processes are combining to leave some of the poorest, sickest Americans facing death without care. That’s cruelty with a capital C. The frightening part is that it seems this administration is just getting started.
